1007-divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-pa:
Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy ends in Paradise, translated by the Rev. H. F. Cary into English verse. Beatrice, Dante's guide in Heaven, leads him through the spheres of the blessed, from the moon to the highest heaven, in thirty-three cantos of light, music, and theology.

Cary renders Dante's vision with clarity and grace, as saints, angels, and the poet's own wonder fill each canto. Paradise is the hardest and most radiant part of the Comedy, and Cary's version helps English readers follow its ascent. The book completes the journey begun in Hell, and it rewards patient, awed reading.
10383-the-maternal-management-of-childre:
Thomas Bull, a London physician and lecturer on midwifery, published this guide for young mothers in 1840. Bull warns that most mothers lack plain facts about infant care, and that ignorance can injure a child's health for life. His book aims to prevent disease, not to teach mothers to cure it alone.

Early chapters cover feeding, dress, air, and daily care in health, while later chapters teach parents to spot the first signs of illness and seek prompt help. Bull stresses caution with medicine. Readers get a clear, period manual of Victorian child care, dated in advice, but humane in intent.
10441-the-green-mouse:
Robert W. Chambers published this romance in 1910, with color pictures by Edmund Frederick. Chambers, known for lighter fiction as well as mystery, opens with a playful dedication on folly and wisdom as heavenly twins. The book treats idleness, love, and imagination with wit and ease.

Chapters follow an idler, an idyl of the idle, the green mouse itself, an ideal idol, and a figure called Sacharissa, through wrong turns and an invisible wire. Love and fancy, rather than war or crime, drive the plot. Readers get a charming, whimsical novel of young people, art, and romance in the 1910s.
10585-my-strangest-case:
Guy Boothby, author of Dr. Nikola and Pharos the Egyptian, published this mystery in 1901, opening in Singapore. Boothby calls Singapore a study of human life, where British rule meets the Chinese question, half the world's tongues sound in an hour's walk, and smells range from lotus to durian. The harbor and streets set a vivid, exotic stage.

A dark, narrow hole, a Bank of England note in each hand, a poor devil on his last legs, and a revolver in hand fill the illustrations. Gregory and other figures drive a strange case of crime and fate. Readers get a lively, period thriller of the East, full of color, suspense, and Boothby's brisk style.
10596-cap-and-gown-a-treasury-of-college:
Frederic Lawrence Knowles gathered Cap and Gown in 1897 as a treasury of verse about undergraduate life. Dedicated to the memory of the scholar Francis James Child, the book collects light, graceful poems by many hands, most of them young men and women at college. Its editor warns that such verse should not be judged as high poetry.

The poems sing of youth, joy, love, sport, friendship, and the edge of adult duty, with humor and sparkle rather than gloom. Serious notes appear, but only in passing, as befits writers on the verge of grown life. Readers get a charming anthology of student days in late nineteenth-century America.
10607-the-real-mother-goose:
The Real Mother Goose, published in 1916 with pictures by Blanche Fisher Wright, collects the nursery rhymes every English-speaking child once knew by heart. Little Bo-Peep, Little Boy Blue, Pat-a-Cake, Georgy Porgy, Wee Willie Winkie, and dozens more fill its pages, from counting rhymes to lullabies and riddles.

Wright's color illustrations give each rhyme a warm, old-fashioned scene, and the book is made to be read aloud at bedtime. The rhymes themselves carry centuries of nonsense, warning, and play. Families still use this edition as a first book of verse, and it remains a standard gift for young children.
10727-a-set-of-rogues-namely-christopher:
Frank Barrett published A Set of Rogues in 1895 as the faithful confession of Christopher Sutton, one of four rogues whose conspiracy drives the tale. Sutton, John Dawson, Don Sanchez, and Moll Dawson plot a marriage by sinful means for Moll to a worthy gentleman, then follow her fall, remorse, and second expedition into strange places. Her atonement to Mr. Richard Godwin closes the circle.

The rogues' path leads to Algerine pirates, Barbary slavery, and tribulations for all who led Moll astray. Barrett writes in the manner of old rogue tales, with high adventure and moral reckoning. Readers get a swashbuckling story of crime, repentance, and escape, told with period charm.
10954-the-girl-aviators-sky-cruise:
Margaret Burnham's 1911 adventure returns to Peggy Prescott and her friends at Sandy Beach. A big new red building with skylights puzzles the neighbourhood, and its owner, Mr. Harding, soon draws the young aviators into a scheme involving a naval visitor, stolen drawings, and a rival flying machine called the Silver Cobweb. Roy, Jess, and Jimsy share the work and the danger.

Storms aloft, a marked bill, a captured brother, and an aerial post office keep the plot moving toward a long sky cruise. Peggy proves steady in a crisis more than once, and the friends foil a plot by watching, flying, and thinking fast. The book gave early readers a heroine who flew her own machine and solved problems in the air.
11095-fun-and-nonsense:
Willard Bonte wrote and illustrated this small book of nonsense verses, where household objects and foods come alive and talk. Chocolate Drop the barber asks a stick of peppermint to be his barber pole, a whitewash brush gives up combing its pompadour hair, and old Mr. Match scratches his head and lights up the dark with his spark. A lettuce loses its head, a pumpkin explains greenness, and a pocketbook refuses loans.

Other verses follow Dr. Yeast-Cake, Pilot Von Pretzel the crusty salt tanned in a baking pan, and scissor twins who cut as ever. Pictures face each short poem, making the book a visual joke book for children. Bonte's puns and personifications give young readers light, silly fun, with a new laugh on every page.
11194-vignettes-in-verse:
Matilda Betham published these Vignettes in Verse in 1818, inscribed to Lady Betham as a tribute of respect for her amiable qualities. Betham explains in an advertisement dated May 10, 1818, that the poems to page seventy-four were printed two years earlier, then delayed by many happenings, until she found the remainder. Reading them over, they struck her as strangely prophetic of her own long seclusion.

The opening vignette imagines journals as wings: each pair a day, some rising in sun, others bending mournfully through cold and cloudy skies, some wounded by an arrow from below. Later verses praise maternal care, village girls, and music's art, while a lover tests a lady's mind by her skill at the keyboard. Betham's verses blend reflection, nature imagery, and social observation.
11351-cape-cod-ballads-and-other-verse:
Joseph C. Lincoln's 1902 Cape Cod Ballads and Other Verse, illustrated by Edward W. Kemble, gathers poems of Cape Cod life: the cod-fisher, the song of the sea, the life-saver, Sunday afternoons, old daguerreotypes, the Sunday-school picnic, the tin peddler, and the light-keeper. Lincoln, later famous for Cape Cod novels, writes in dialect and in standard verse by turns, with humor in pieces like the ballad of McCarty's trombone and O'Reilly's billy-goat.

The poems preserve a coastal village world of fishermen, ministers, and summer visitors, affectionate rather than elegiac. Drawings by Kemble add to the period charm. Readers who enjoy regional verse will find Lincoln's Cape Cod already fully formed here, before his novels made it famous.
11557-on-compromise:
John Morley's essay, first printed in 1886 and reissued in 1908, asks whether truth should come first or second in public life. He calls the book an essay only, meant to open questions, point to cases, and sketch outlines, not to settle casuistry as a treatise would.

Chapters take up the possible use of error, intellectual duty against the political spirit, religious conformity, and the realisation of opinion in action. Hume, and the right of resistance kept as a secret doctrine, supply one of his sharpest examples of a mind steering badly after a false start.
11593-the-purchase-price-or-the-cause-of:
Emerson Hough's 1910 novel, The Purchase Price, or The Cause of Compromise, opens with a lady in company and a gateway through which many pass. A question, a game, and spoils of war follow, with a new master and confusion in chattels.

Later chapters bring Tallwoods, free and thrall, garments of another, a night, an invasion, and an argument before an adjudication. A lady at Tallwoods, a man on parole, and an enemy close the middle of the book. The story moves between Kentucky and Washington, and it turns on honour, payment, and the price of compromise in a divided land.
11660-ethel-morton-s-enterprise:
Mabell S. C. Smith's Ethel Morton's Enterprise opens with Ethel Blue, named for her blue eyes, watching January snow fall in large, damp flakes. Her cousin Ethel Brown, brown-eyed, and Dorothy Smith join her, all three with birthdays in January.

Chapters move from a snow man and seed catalogues to gardening on paper, wild flowers for Helen's garden, and colour schemes. Cave life, a flower festival, and a spell in business follow, with Uncle Dan's researches and a missing heiress. The book is a girls' story of gardens, community work, and a small enterprise grown from a winter afternoon.
11857-the-lay-of-marie-and-vignettes-in-:
Matilda Betham's 1816 poem The Lay of Marie anchors this Garland reprint, paired with her 1818 Vignettes in Verse and introduced by Donald H. Reiman. Betham addresses the poem to Lady Bedingfeld and builds it from medieval romance, following Marie, a figure of minstrel lore, through love, honor, and pleading before a king.

The volume also preserves Betham's appendix on Marie herself, including her work translating fables into French verse and the question of how many she rendered from English sources. As a facsimile of copies held at Yale and the British Library, it keeps both the poems and their early nineteenth-century presentation intact.
11936-the-wise-mamma-goose:
Herr's 1913 children's story The Wise Mamma Goose, with designs by Frances Beem, was told and drawn for one good little child. The child's name is left blank on the dedication page for a young owner to fill in. The tale begins with Mamma Goose trying to think, a task made impossible by the noise of the barnyard.

She hides herself between rows of tall red hollyhocks bordering one side of the yard, where she can collect her wits in quiet. Herr's simple prose and Beem's pictures suit very young readers. The story's humor lies in its modest premise: even a goose needs peace and a little privacy before she can think clearly.
1196-the-purse:
Honoré de Balzac tells a short, tender tale of a young painter who lodges with a poor widow and her daughter, and who falls in love as he paints. The daughter embroiders him a purse, a small gift that carries her whole heart, and pride, poverty, and kindness tangle around it.

Balzac writes Parisian life with his usual eye for rooms, clothes, and small sums of money, and the story ends with a quiet, bittersweet turn. The tale is slight beside his great novels, but its feeling is true. It suits readers who like Balzac in miniature.
11965-sex-and-common-sense:
A. Maude Royden, assistant preacher at the City Temple, London, in 1918 to 1920, published Sex and Common-Sense as a frank discussion of the relations of the sexes. Royden opens with the nobility of the sex problem. She notes that no problem occupies the alert modern mind more, since it touches us all and we have made rather a mess of it.

The book asks why relations between men and women go wrong and what common sense, as distinct from prudery or license, would suggest. Royden, a pioneering woman preacher and suffragist, writes for readers willing to discuss sex openly and morally. Her book captures a moment when churches and feminists alike were rethinking sexual ethics.
1199-an-anthology-of-australian-verse:
Bertram Stevens edits an anthology of Australian verse, gathering poems that give the young nation's voice in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Bush ballads, lyrics, and city poems sit side by side. Stevens, an Australian editor, gathered verse from a colony becoming a nation.

Stevens chooses work that shows Australia's landscape, history, and humour, from frontier tales to quiet lyrics. The anthology remains a useful first survey of Australian poetry for readers outside the country. The anthology includes bush ballads that Australians still sing and quote today. Stevens's choices shaped how later readers pictured Australian verse.
11999-the-servant-in-the-house:
Charles Rann Kennedy's play The Servant in the House, published in 1908 and dedicated to Walter Hampden, belongs to a set of seven plays for seven players. Kennedy's other volumes in the series include The Winterfeast, The Idol-Breaker. The Rib of the Man, with shorter plays such as The Terrible Meek and The Necessary Evil.

The play opens in a vicarage household, where Manson the servant serves breakfast in silence and answers questions about the Bishop of Benares. The Bishop himself demands a private interview with Manson, insisting that the peace and security of a human soul depends on it. Kennedy uses the servant, a stranger in the house, to test the household's faith, in a drama of revelation rather than of plot twists.
1235-captain-fracasse:
Théophile Gautier's romance follows the Baron de Sigognac, a penniless noble who joins a troupe of strolling players and takes the stage name Captain Fracasse. The road brings sword fights, love, and intrigue, as the baron woos the actress Isabelle and duels a rival duke.

Gautier writes seventeenth-century France in rich, swashbuckling color, with inns, castles, and snowbound roads. The novel mixes theatre lore with cloak-and-dagger adventure. It remains a beloved French classic, and it still delights readers who love romance with a sword in hand.
12423-a-short-history-of-the-united-stat:
Edward Channing, professor of history at Harvard, wrote this 1908 school history with maps and illustrations. A Lowell verse on Lincoln fronts the volume, praising a kindly, earnest, brave and foreseeing man, a new birth of new soil. The history then moves in order, from discovery and exploration to colonisation and beyond.

Contents run from Spanish and French pioneers through Virginia, Maryland, New England, New Netherland and New Sweden, then through a century of colonial life. Channing writes in a clear, textbook manner for pupils, with narrative and dates kept in balance. The volume offers a period view of American history as schools taught it before the First World War.
12674-cock-lane-and-common-sense:
Andrew Lang's Cock Lane and Common-Sense, dedicated to James Payn, defends folklore study of ghosts and marvels. Lang tells Payn that spirits rarer than those in the book are his, since Payn transfers high spirits to readers. He hopes his work may bring a smile to his favourite novelist's lips.

A preface notes that since first publication in 1894, nothing has greatly altered Lang's opinions. He tried to make the Folklore Society see modern reports of wraiths, ghosts, fire-walking, corpse-lights and crystal-gazing as within its province. Lang writes with wit and scepticism, balancing belief and doubt. The book is a classic of psychical research, charming and argumentative.
1304-bulchevy-s-book-of-english-verse:
An English verse survey, previously released as the Oxford Book of English Verse, gathers lyrics from Chaucer onward in one broad sweep. The editor's choice, under the name Bulchevy, follows the Oxford tradition of taste. The Oxford Book of English Verse, edited by Arthur Quiller-Couch, set the standard anthology.

Poems of love, nature, war, and faith appear in chronological order, letting readers trace English poetry across centuries. The volume works as a single-shelf anthology for anyone who wants the main line of English verse. This Gutenberg version, renamed for trademark reasons, follows the same broad survey.
13052-the-mistress-of-the-manse:
J. G. Holland's 1874 poem in narrative verse tells of a pastor and his wife, Philip and Mildred, arriving at a new manse. Its sections run from a prelude through love's experiments, philosophies, and consummations. Holland writes in rhymed stanzas, with domestic scenes set against storms, willows, and midnight rain.

The poem follows the wife as she grows from a shy bride into the true mistress of the house, skilled with pin and spool, hands that help and words that bless. Her husband learns to see her full worth only over time. The Mistress of the Manse is a gentle, old-fashioned love poem about marriage as a slow education in respect.
13546-the-dark-house:
I. A. R. Wylie's 1922 novel The Dark House opens with small Robert Stonehouse leaning from an upstairs bedroom window on his birthday, suddenly eight years old in feeling. He once danced on his mother's bed shouting I'm five, while his father, who did things in style, gave him a toy fort garrisoned with resplendent Highlanders.

Cosgrave breathes heavily through his nose and whispers shamefacedly that he loves Robert, an awful and wonderful thing to have said, answered with a scolding about silly girls. Gertie Sumners, Howard, and a faun dancing among shadows fill later scenes, as Robert tries to hold back feeling in a room against him. Wylie writes childhood, friendship, and a dark house of memory.
13612-studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-v:
The third volume of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex was revised and enlarged in 1927. It holds three studies: the analysis of the sexual impulse, love and pain, and the sexual impulse in women. Ellis draws on physiology, case histories, and letters from readers to build a picture of desire as a natural force with wide variation.

He examines how passion works in men and women, why pain and love sometimes join, and why women often seem colder than they are, naming repression, disease, and social training as causes. The tone is clinical and even, and Ellis resists both prudery and sensationalism. The volume stands as a serious early attempt to describe female sexuality from evidence rather than from custom.
13646-a-book-of-nonsense:
Edward Lear's Book of Nonsense holds all original pictures and verses. It opens with an old Derry down Derry who loved to see little folks merry and made them a book at which they shook with laughter. Lear dedicates the drawings and verses to the great-grandchildren, grand-nephews, and grand-nieces of Edward, thirteenth Earl of Derby, for whose parents most were first made.

Limericks follow in quick succession: a young lady of Norway squeezed flat in a doorway, an old man of Apulia feeding twenty sons on buns. An old man of Quebec slaying a beetle with a needle, a small man who buys a wig to look big, and a young lady of Russia whose screams none could hush. Lear's nonsense is brief, musical, and drawn with the verses.
13648-more-nonsense:
Edward Lear's More Nonsense gathers nonsense botany, one hundred nonsense pictures and rhymes, and twenty-six more rhymes and pictures. Barkia Howlaloudia, Enkoopia Chickabiddia, Jinglia Tinkettlia, Nasticreechia Krorluppia, and Shoebootia Utilis name plants that never grew, drawn with mock scientific care.

Limericks follow: an old person of Hove studying books with wrens and rooks, a young person in pink offered only water to drink. An old lady of France teaching ducklings to dance, an old person of Hyde frightened by a crab on the shore, and an old person in grey feeding parrots carrots. Lear's later nonsense keeps the same recipe: a place, a person, and a small absurd twist.
1369-paz-la-fausse-maitresse:
Honoré de Balzac tells of Paz, a Polish exile who serves his friend Laginski with devotion, and who secretly loves Laginski's wife, Clémentine. To hide his love, Paz pretends a mistress, and the false affair tangles the household in jealousy and misunderstanding.

Balzac writes Parisian society with his usual eye for money, rank, and feeling, and Paz's silent suffering gives the tale its ache. The story is short and poignant. It suits readers who like Balzac's tales of love kept secret and honor kept hard. Paz's silent suffering gives Balzac's short tale its ache.
13877-poise:
D. Starke wrote Poise: How to Attain It as part of a Mental Efficiency series, translated by Francis Medhurst in 1916. Starke defines poise as power derived from mastery of self. Part one covers its need, its enemies, and war on timidity. Part two gives physical and practical exercises for gaining poise.

Chapters contrast modesty with effrontery and list four series of physical exercises. Starke describes timid people who lose ideas at the thought of contest, however courteous. Practice, he argues, builds calm presence step by step. The book reflects early self-help writing before modern psychology. It offers simple drills for readers who fear public situations.
14293-the-complete-book-of-cheese:
Bob Brown wrote this 1955 book of cheese, with pictures by Eric Blegvad. It tours cheeses of many lands, from foreign greats to native American kinds. Recipes follow: soufflés, fondues, pizzas, rarebit, and sixty-five sizzling rabbits. Brown writes as a cook who loves cheese and loves a joke. The book serves both as a guide to buying and as a cookery book for the table.

A cheese-potato soufflé shows the method: potatoes and onions riced, mixed with milk, Cheddar, and eggs, then baked till puffed and gold. A long glossary names cheeses land by land, from Belgian cooked cheese to Corsican Roquefort copies and Caucasus brined kinds. Cornimont of the Vosges gets praise as a fine Alsatian Münster spiked with caraway. The book mixes lore, shopping notes, and kitchen craft in one cheerful volume.
14485-notes-on-the-apocalypse:
David Steele Sr., pastor of the Reformed Presbyterian congregation in Philadelphia, published these Notes on the Apocalypse in 1870, with an appendix on apocalyptic symbols. He wrote to a fellow minister in London.

Steele works verse by verse through Revelation, from the trumpets and the Euphrates angels to the harvest of wrath, and he disputes the readings of learned British and American expositors. His historicist view ties symbols to the Roman empire and later powers. The book is a dense specimen of nineteenth-century Reformed prophecy study, earnest and systematic. Steele's congregation in Philadelphia heard these readings preached first.
14506-the-white-linen-nurse:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott's 1913 novel centers on a weary hospital nurse, known only as the White Linen Nurse, whose fixed sickroom smile aches along with her feet. Abbott dedicated the book to a surgeon who loved romance.

The nurse takes charge of a sharp-tongued little girl, trades letters with Dr. Faber, and finds her professional calm tested by a child's candor and a grown man's courtship. Abbott writes in a bright, comic voice, full of dialogue and hospital detail. The novel is a light romance of duty and feeling, popular in its day and still charming.
14553-a-catechism-of-christian-doctrine-:
Baltimore Catechism No. 3, for a two-year course for post-confirmation classes, supplemented by the Reverend Thomas L. Kinkead and published by Benziger Brothers, expands the shorter catechisms for older pupils. It follows the new canon law.

Later questions treat the Church's indefectibility and infallibility, distinguishing a Church that lasts forever from one that cannot teach error. The volume carries the 1885 and 1901 imprimaturs. It served advanced classes with fuller doctrine, and it remains the fullest of the Baltimore catechisms for study. Kinkead's supplement answered questions older pupils actually asked in class.
1461-a-legend-of-montrose:
Walter Scott's tale of the Scottish Civil War follows the Marquis of Montrose and his Highland allies as they fight for the king against the Covenanters. At its centre stands Sergeant More M'Alpin and a band of outlaw Children of the Mist, whose clan loyalties cut across the armies of the day.

Through marches, skirmishes, and a tangled love plot, Scott weighs honour, revenge, and the claims of kin against those of a cause. Notes and an appendix on clan custom round out the tale. It is a brisk, romantic piece of Scott's Tales of My Landlord manner, full of Highland colour.
14781-the-elene-of-cynewulf-translated-i:
Lucius Hudson Holt's 1904 prose translation brings Cynewulf's Old English poem Elene to modern readers, in Yale Studies in English. The poem tells how Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine, seeks the True Cross in Jerusalem.

Constantine's story frames the quest. In his sixth year as Roman ruler, he faces Huns, Goths and Franks in battle, and his rise is told in the language of shields, spears and loyalty to his men. Elene then turns from war to search and discovery, joining history, legend and faith. Holt keeps the poem's plain narrative force, so readers can follow an early English saint's life without learning the old tongue.
1484-the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse:
Vicente Blasco Ibanez's great war novel follows the Desnoyers family, French and German by marriage. It runs from a Paris garden tryst through the years before 1914 to the trenches of the First World War. Don Marcelo, a rich Argentine landowner, watches his sons and cousins take opposite sides in a war that tears his house apart.

The four horsemen of the title ride through the book as symbols of conquest, war, famine, and death, and the novel's battle scenes carry real horror. Translated by Charlotte Brewster Jordan, it was a worldwide bestseller. It remains a powerful, if melodramatic, portrait of a family at war.
15094-the-cab-of-the-sleeping-horse:
John Reed Scott's 1916 mystery novel opens late at night in a Washington club, where talk turns to a clever and lovely woman with many names. Harleston, one of the clubmen, knows her past: a failed marriage, a ruined young officer, and a trail of bold deceits. The talk soon gives way to action.

From photographs and phone calls to taxis, coded words, and a grey-stone house, the plot unwinds through surprise meetings and near escapes. Madeline Cuthbert, under her shifting names, stays at the center of the chase. The novel offers period intrigue, brisk dialogue, and a heroine who is as dangerous as she is charming.
15102-proposals-for-building-in-every-co:
Printed in London in 1677, this pamphlet urges Parliament to build a working almshouse in every English county. Its author argues that the poor, including children from five or six years old, could be set to making linen cloth instead of living on parish relief. Beggars and vagrants would be put to useful work as well.

Three gains are claimed: parishes eased of a heavy burden, money kept at home instead of spent on foreign linen, and waste land improved to grow flax. The plan blends charity, discipline, and trade policy in a very seventeenth-century mix. Modern readers will find it a sharp window onto early ideas about poverty and work.
15124-the-lighthouse:
R. M. Ballantyne's adventure novel tells of Ruby, a young man drawn into the building of a lighthouse on the Bell Rock off Scotland. Press-gangs, a burglary, storms, and smugglers cross his path before he reaches the rock itself. Chapters follow the work crew through tides, fog, and narrow escapes.

Ballantyne, known for The Coral Island, writes with a seaman's eye for ships, tools, and weather, and with a moral warmth toward his hero. Life in the beacon, the story of Eddystone, and the battle of Arbroath all find room. Boys' adventure fans will find the book brisk, brave, and full of sea detail.
15308-nitro-explosives-a-practical-treat:
P. Gerald Sanford's Nitro-Explosives, in a second revised edition, is a practical treatise on nitrated substances, including fulminates, smokeless powders, and celluloid. Sanford served as public analyst for Penzance and chemist to powder firms at Stowmarket and Hayle. A danger building with protecting mounds fronts the book.

Chapters explain properties, manufacture, and analysis of explosives, with safety and testing in view. The preface promises a working handbook, not a popular survey. Chemists, engineers, and historians of industry will find the treatise detailed, technical, and very much a product of its dangerous trade.
15492-a-doll-s-house:
Henrik Ibsen's play, in the Haldeman-Julius Ten Cent Pocket Series edition of 1923, is set entirely in the Helmer house. The cast lists Torvald Helmer, his wife Nora, Doctor Rank, Mrs. Linde, Nils Krogstad, three young children, a nurse, a maid, and a porter. Act One opens in winter, in a room furnished comfortably but not extravagantly, with a fire burning.

Nora enters humming, in high spirits, carrying parcels, and the play follows her secret and its slow exposure. A letter box, a heap of letters, and Doctor Rank's cards marked with a black cross raise the stakes act by act. Ibsen's drama turns on marriage, debt, and a woman's claim to a self apart from her husband's house. Its closing break remains one of modern theatre's most debated moments.
15550-ethel-morton-at-rose-house:
Mabell S. C. Smith published this girls' story in 1915, with the World Syndicate Publishing Company in Cleveland and New York, in the Juvenile Library Girls Series. A frontispiece cries, Here's where we should land. The story follows Ethel Brown Morton and her cousin Ethel Blue, two girls who share a first name and much else.

Chapter one, Roger's Idea, finds the two Ethels untangling maypole garlands for the fortieth time that afternoon, guiding small children in and out among pink and white bands. May Day in New Jersey may recall the North Pole or the Equator, and this day is the hottest of the year so far. Later pages bring a chimney fall, dynamite cartridges in a trash fire, and a brickmason's call. The book mixes club life, mishaps, and friendship in a New Jersey town.
15965-in-friendship-s-guise:
A mystery novel by Wm. Murray Graydon, author of The Cryptogram, issued in 1899. Graydon writes of art, friendship, and betrayal in London and Paris. A duplicate Rembrandt opens the tale, with five years afterwards bringing an old friend back. The plot moves through Wardour Street, Pall Mall, and Richmond dinners.

A visitor from Paris, love's young dream, and an uncle and nephew tangle the threads. A London sensation, a mysterious discovery, and a cowardly communication follow, with a tempter at work. From the dead, the last card, and two passengers from Calais close the game. The novel delights as a Victorian mystery: friendship worn as a guise, and truth found at last.
1719-the-ballad-of-the-white-horse:
King Alfred, beaten and doubting, gathers a broken people against Danish invaders in this ballad of the White Horse of the Berkshire downs. Chesterton warns in his prefatory note that the poem does not claim to be history: what is not frankly invented is meant to stress tradition rather than fact.

Alfred, facing the Danes, gathers a beaten people and leads them against invaders who fill the land like seas of spears. The poem's refrain is England itself, deepening like a garden toward Wales, and its hero is a king who doubts, prays, and fights on. It remains Chesterton's most ambitious poem, and a patriotic work that never turns simple.
1727-the-odyssey-rendered-into-english-p:
Odysseus has been held by the nymph Calypso since the fall of Troy. This prose version follows his ten-year road home, while Penelope holds off suitors in Ithaca. Odysseus, held by the nymph Calypso after the fall of Troy, sails home across ten years of storms, monsters, and strange shores. Meanwhile his wife Penelope holds off suitors in Ithaca, and his son Telemachus searches for news of him.

The prose keeps the story's shape intact: the Cyclops, Circe, the Sirens, the underworld, and the final contest of the bow. For a first reading of the epic, this version offers a clear path through all twenty-four books without verse to slow it down. The tale's mix of cunning, endurance, and homecoming comes through undimmed.
1760-the-man-who-could-not-lose:
Richard Harding Davis opens with the Carters, married in haste and refusing to repent at leisure, whose love the world counts as their only asset. The title story follows a man whose luck at cards and horses never fails him. Then a dream of a horse named Dromedary repeats night after night, and his friends begin to wonder what the luck is costing him.

Davis writes about gamblers, sportsmen, and society folk with the ease of a man who knew their world. The stories turn on chance, nerve, and the moment luck turns. The collection is light, brisk, and of its period. Its best moments come when a character must decide whether to trust a run of fortune or walk away from the table.
1807-the-lost-house:
On a dull day at a chancellery, with the ambassador away unveiling a bust of Burns, a mystery arrives in the form of a house that cannot be found. Into the quiet steps a mystery: a house that cannot be found and a paper unrolled by a coal fire. A man named Ford snatches the paper from the flame.

Davis builds the tale from diplomatic rooms and small, watched details, and its interest lies in what a scrap of paper can mean when nations are involved. The story is short and tense, and it shows Davis using his knowledge of embassies to give a small incident the weight of an affair of state.
1904-the-life-and-perambulations-of-a-mo:
Dorothy Kilner's Life and Perambulations of a Mouse, was written in 1783 and 1784. It tells the adventures of a mouse through a remarkably severe winter, when a prodigious fall of snow confined everybody to their houses. The mouse narrator, kept awake by fresh terrors, spends a day in almost total silence, having no spirits for conversation.

Kilner writes for children, and the mouse's journeys through kitchens, parlors, and traps become lessons in caution, kindness, and the dangers of curiosity. The book is one of the earliest animal autobiographies in English. Its small scale — a mouse's eye view of a household — gives it a charm that later books of the kind have copied.
19672-the-holladay-case:
Burton E. Stevenson was an American writer of mystery and adventure stories. The Holladay Case is one of his detective tales. It opens in a law office thrown into alarm. A junior clerk named Royce bursts in, shaken and distracted. He carries a newspaper that has clearly stunned him. His employer Graham wheels from his desk in astonishment.

A shocked entrance promises a death or disgrace in the headlines. Stevenson liked legal settings, secrets, and patient unraveling. His detectives work through talk, papers, and close observation. The opening puts all three in play within a page. Readers who like early American detective fiction will find the period machinery here.
19945-bakemono-yashiki-the-haunted-house:
Bakemono Yashiki means the haunted house, or goblin house, in Japanese. James de Benneville retold it from Japanese sources. Like its companion volumes, it leans on Edo maps of 1857 and 1866. Street plans from the Go Edo Zusetsu Shuran fill out the setting. A haunted house needs a real address to chill properly. De Benneville supplies Edo in detail around his ghosts.

Bakemono are shape-changing beings of Japanese folklore. Tales about them blend terror with sly humor. De Benneville collected such stories while living in Japan. His retellings introduced many Western readers to Japanese ghost lore. The topographical fussiness is part of his charm. Haunting, here, is a matter of record.
1997-the-divine-comedy-volume-3-paradise:
Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy closes with Paradise, in Charles Eliot Norton's translation, where Beatrice guides Dante upward through the spheres of heaven. The cantos move from the Moon, where spirits whose vows were broken dwell, through Mercury, Venus, and the Sun, toward the vision of God.

Beatrice explains the cause of the ascent, the spots on the Moon, and the influence of the heavens, and Dante's questions grow deeper as he rises. Norton's translation keeps the poem's argument clear. The volume completes a journey that began in Hell: from sin through purgation to a light that words can barely hold.
2002-sonnets-from-the-portuguese:
Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote these forty-four sonnets as a private record of her courtship with Robert Browning, first passed off as translations from Portuguese. The sequence moves from doubt and grief to trust and deep love. Browning first shared the sonnets with her husband alone, and they reached print only after friends urged publication.

Each sonnet speaks in the first person, weighing what love can give and what it costs, and the best-known lines still turn up in weddings and anthologies. Read straight through, the poems form a single love story told in tight, musical verse. The Portuguese disguise let a Victorian woman speak of love with a frankness her age seldom allowed in public.
20085-the-tragic-muse:
Henry James published The Tragic Muse, a novel about art, theatre, and English society. James writes of a race whose energy strikes foreign eyes with force. Some feel awe at it, others feel sharp dislike instead. That cool, exact eye marks the whole book from the start.

The tragic muse is the stage muse, and acting drives the tale. A young woman must weigh art against the safe life society offers. James traces small shifts of mind with great care and depth. Readers get one of his rich studies of ambition, love, and the price of art.
20511-the-little-mother-goose:
The Little Mother Goose, published in 1912, gathers the classic nursery rhymes for very young children. It presents them with pictures in color and in black and white. The rhymes are the ones English-speaking children have learned for centuries.

Here is the old riddle rhyme of the road to St. Ives. As I was going to St. Ives, I met a man with seven wives. Every wife had seven sacks, every sack had seven cats, and every cat had seven kits. Generations of children have puzzled over how many were going to St. Ives.
20767-the-life-of-mansie-wauch-tailor-in:
Mansie Wauch, a tailor in Dalkeith, tells his own life in broad Scots. He recalls his grandfather, a tall old man with white locks and rose-red cheeks. Blind with age, the old man still sits clear in the boy's early memory.

David Macbeth Moir wrote this famed Scots tale of small-town life. Mansie bumbles, boasts, and repents through work, love, and local fame. The dialect gives the book its warmth and much of its fun. Readers meet a Scotland of kirks, fairs, and sharp tongues, seen through one vain but kind heart, drawn with love and gentle mockery.
20984-prudy-keeping-house:
Dotty with eyes like living diamonds watches a snowstorm as Prudy Keeping House opens. Prudy, fair and sweet, begs Horace to shut the window before the plants freeze. Sophie May peoples her tale with the famed Clarke children in bright strokes.

Prudy, the eldest girl, tries her hand at keeping house in this tale. Sophie May, whose real name was Rebecca Clarke, wrote the Prudy books for young girls. Dishes, guests, and small disasters test Prudy's young charge. The set charmed post-Civil War homes with its true talk, warm humour, and sisters drawn from life as their author knew it.
21217-the-one-moss-rose:
Leonard Dobbin, a poor labourer on Squire Courtenay's estate, keeps a humble cottage that is a pattern of neatness. The Reverend P. B. Power's 1872 story centres on Dobbin's one luxury, his little flower garden. The pride of that garden is a moss-rose tree.

The rose belongs in a special way to Dobbin's crippled little son Jacob. He watches it from the window and creeps out when he can to water it and pick off snails. No mother, the story says, watched a baby more eagerly than Jacob watched his rose. Power builds a gentle moral tale around the flower and the boy.
21317-a-life-s-eclipse:
John Grange, an under-gardener on Mrs Mostyn's estate, loves Mary Ellis, the bailiff's daughter. Her father James Ellis is angry that a mere gardener dares think of her. George Manville Fenn then drops a tree on John's ambitions: sent up a great cedar to tidy a broken bough, he falls on his head.

John recovers from the concussion blind. His rival Daniel Barnett takes the head gardener's post John might have had. Barnett plays cruel tricks on him, though blind John still works well by touch. When John vanishes without trace, rumour accuses Barnett of making away with him. Fenn saves the truth for a surprise ending.
21358-the-ocean-cat-s-paw-the-story-of-a:
Rodd, a Devon boy fishing a Dartmoor stream, hides a young Frenchman who has just escaped from the Dartmoor prison camp of the Napoleonic Wars. George Manville Fenn then sends Rodd's uncle to sea on a government grant. The uncle, a doctor and natural history researcher, is to buy a ship and collect specimens. Rodd sails with him.

Bad weather drives them into a French port, and later they meet a strange brig holed below the waterline in a fight. Her officers prove to be the escaped boy and his father, a count. British seamanship patches the hole. The strange cruise of the title ranges far beyond one act of boyish mercy.
21446-favourite-fables-in-prose-and-vers:
Favourite Fables, in prose and verse, was printed in London in 1870 with drawings by Harrison Weir. The set opens with the fox and the goat, where a fox falls into a well. He swims from side to side and cannot climb out by his own pains.

Twenty-four pictures back a run of short, famed tales for the young. Readers meet the frog and the ox, the dove and the ant, and the frogs who wanted a king. Other fables treat the fox without a tail and the horse and the stag. Each ends with its lesson plainly drawn, in the old manner.
21541-quiet-please:
Groverzb wants only peace and quiet in Kevin Scott's short tale Quiet Please, from Worlds of If in November 1961. He is willing to scream his head off to get it, as the blurb jokes. A big porter lugs his piano in and warns him he will not like the planet.

The natives stand no more than three feet tall and never talk aloud. That silence is just why Groverzb, who loathes conversation, has come. His house is a gutted block once home to the Little People. By evening a violet glow falls, small folk dash below, and no voice breaks the calm he craves.
2161-the-song-book-of-quong-lee-of-limeh:
Thomas Burke gives voice to Quong Lee, a Chinese shopkeeper in London's Limehouse, in short pieces on buying and selling, music, lamplighters, shop windows, and the feast of lanterns. Each song is brief and vivid. Burke wrote of Limehouse from visits to its shops, cafes, and docks.

Quong Lee watches English life with a stranger's clear eye, on gambling, politicians, war, and worship, and his notes mix humour with quiet sadness. The book offers a rare early portrait of London's Chinese quarter from inside its streets. Quong Lee's songs, short and sharp, read like notes jotted between customers.
21618-the-aztec-treasure-house:
Thomas Allibone Janvier hunts Montezuma's gold in The Aztec Treasure-House, copyrighted in 1890. A verse at the front promises marvels, hidden gold, and gallant fights. Fray Antonio and a dying cacique hold the first clues to the hoard.

A monk's manuscript and Montezuma's messenger guide the seekers into Mexico. Chapters pass a submerged city, a swinging statue, and a cave of the dead. The Chac-Mool stair and a temple in the clouds raise the stakes. Janvier, who lived in Mexico and loved its lore, packs the tale with real learning worn lightly throughout.
21740-the-iron-horse:
Trains shake the house where little Gertie lives in this Ballantyne tale of the railways. Her father, John Marrot, is an engine driver, and the passing trains rattle her bed curtains day and night. Gertie is six, rosy, and sweet, with a mind very much her own. She saves her kisses for a chosen few, her father first among them.

Ballantyne researched the railways as he did each trade he wrote about. The tale shows engine crews, their homes, their risks, and their pride in the iron horse. Domestic warmth and real danger share the chapters. It gives young readers a close, kind look at the men who ran the steam age.
21746-the-lighthouse:
Two fishermen row out from Forfarshire on a still summer morning at the start of this Ballantyne tale. The sea lies like glass, and the big, rough-spoken boatman jokes that the calm will help them land on the rock. That rock, far from shore, is where a lighthouse must rise. The work ahead will test builders, sailors, and engineers alike.

Ballantyne tells how such lights were built on wave-washed rocks at the start of the nineteenth century. He mixes the building work with the lives of the men who did it. Storms fight the work at every stage. The finished light stands as proof of patience, skill, and plain courage.
21998-the-lion-s-mouse:
A hard man is caught in a net of his own making in The Lion's Mouse, a 1919 novel by C. N. and A. M. Williamson. Roger Sands has steel-gray eyes, brows drawn low and nearly meeting, and an aggressive clean-shaven chin. He has the air of being hard as nails. Then a young and beautiful woman hovers at his door, breathing perfume, and begs him to help her.

The contents run in fable order: the lion, the net, the mouse. The queen's pearls, a parcel with gold seals, a bluff that failed and a bluff that won fill the middle. Murder and a brown trunk darken the later chapters. The Williamsons wrote sleek society thrillers as a husband-and-wife team. This one turns Aesop's fable into a romance of rescue.
22246-the-upper-berth-by-the-waters-of-p:
Two long tales by F. Marion Crawford share this volume: The Upper Berth and By the Waters of Paradise. Crawford, an American novelist who lived in Italy, wrote ghost stories of rare polish. The Upper Berth is his most famous. A traveller shares a stateroom with something that will not stay dead, and the ship's officers must be convinced cabin by cabin.

The narrator of the second tale recalls a dinner conversation so boring it would have bored Prometheus on his rock. From that frame the paradise story unfolds. Crawford's horror is quiet, seamanlike, and exact. The Upper Berth still sails through anthologies as one of the finest sea-ghost stories ever written.
22265-frank-merriwell-s-cruise:
Frank Merriwell's Cruise belongs to the dime-novel series that made Frank Merriwell America's model schoolboy. Street and Smith published the tale in 1898, in the Merriwell stories written chiefly by Gilbert Patten. A well-dressed youth pays his cabbie silently and walks into a hotel. A boy takes his bag; he steps to the clerk's desk and speaks, and the adventure is under way.

Merriwell's cruise takes him by yacht into scrapes, rescues, and sporting contests. He never drinks, never swears, and never loses his temper or a game that matters. Millions of boys followed his cruises and campaigns. This number is pure Merriwell: clean, brisk, and perfectly sure of its hero.
22418-dollars-and-sense:
Colonel W. C. Hunter wrote Dollars and Sense, published in 1908. It is a book of business counsel for working readers. Hunter promises a welcome to those who are square, ambitious, and patient.

These chapters, he says, will be old friends to such readers. A few minutes or a few hours both serve for reading. Readers may return as often as they wish, he adds. Each return visit will impress some new truth, he promises. The book belongs to the self-help shelf of its decade. Its lessons join money sense to character and patience. Modern readers get period business advice in a bluff, friendly voice.
22474-fringilla-some-tales-in-verse:
Richard Doddridge Blackmore wrote Fringilla, some tales in verse. Blackmore, the novelist of Lorna Doone, here turns to rhymed storytelling. One tale gives a curious legend on the origin of jealousy.

When Adam and Eve lived in Paradise, the tale begins, Adam withdrew at evening. He retired to the garden's recesses for prayer each night. On one occasion, the Devil appeared to Eve alone. Her solitude, he claimed, was owed to another fair one. Eve replied that it could not possibly be so. She was, she noted, the only woman in existence. That neat logic gives the legend its dry, comic bite.
22657-steam-its-generation-and-use:
Steam: Its Generation and Use is a handbook of steam engineering, first issued by a leading boiler maker and kept in print for decades; this entry holds the 1919 edition. The catalog record names no author. In the steam age, such a book sat in every power plant, part textbook and part company catalog.

The front matter lists offices from Adelaide to St. Petersburg, a map of world industry in itself. Inside, engineers found the physics of heat, the chemistry of boiler water, and rules for safe, thrifty firing. The book taught a trade as much as it sold boilers. It remains a standard period source on how the world made power before electricity took over.
22820-the-crooked-house:
Brandon Fleming's 1921 mystery novel The Crooked House opens with a fright on a dim street. The Right Honorable John Tranter turns, latch-key in hand, as an enormous figure slips noiselessly from the shadow of the next house. The figure's sheer size, grotesque in the lamplight, startles Tranter back.

From that eerie meeting, Fleming builds a tale of crime and pursuit in postwar London. Tranter and the giant stranger stand at the heart of the puzzle, and the crooked house of the title gathers the threads. The writing favors atmosphere, sudden reveals, and cliff-edge chapter ends. Readers who like Golden Age detection in a popular, fast-moving vein will find the machinery they expect, well oiled.
22872-susan-clegg-and-a-man-in-the-house:
Anne Warner's Susan Clegg had lived alone since her father's death, and not unhappily. She had been a good daughter while she had a parent to live with, and she kept her small household in her own firm way. Then, as the title promises, a man comes into the house, and her settled routine meets its test.

Warner built a small comic world around Susan and her friend Mrs. Latham, whose talk carries much of the fun. Dialect, gossip, and stubborn common sense drive these stories more than plot does. The 1906 volume continues a popular series of the day. Readers who enjoy gentle village comedy, told largely in conversation, will feel at home in Susan's parlor.
23030-buying-a-horse:
A friend goes horse shopping in Buying a Horse, a comic sketch of the turf. He walked home encouraged, the narrator says, his purpose seeming less monstrous to a hardened offender in such matters. He began announcing it boldly, claiming he would not go above a hundred, which was not true. Prudence, in his private accounting, meant stretching to a hundred and twenty-five only when driven to it.

Every horse buyer knows that extremity. The sketch follows the bargaining, the vets, the friends with advice, and the horse world's cheerful traps for the earnest novice. Its humor depends on small dishonesties everyone commits. Written when horses still filled the streets, it reads now as both a joke and a document, a field guide to a vanished marketplace.
23037-stories-in-verse:
A flower seller haunts Stories in Verse. One poem fixes its gaze on a flower seller and holds her fast. Lovely as she is, the great town is devouring her in its noise and struggle. How poverty grinds down a life, the poet asks, for what is a beautiful face in the slime of a city?

Verse tales of street life fill this collection of narrative poems. Its subjects are the city's casualties and charmers, told in rhymes meant to be felt quickly. Sentiment was the point, and the poems deliver it without embarrassment. The book preserves the popular poetry of the parlor and the newspaper column, where a flower girl could carry a whole evening's meditation on wealth and beauty.
23069-janet-mclaren-the-faithful-nurse:
Janet McLaren takes charge in Janet McLaren, the Faithful Nurse. The chapter summary tells her work plainly. Janet moves into a small town attic with the children and works to keep them all. Donald and David, the two boys, she manages to place at school. Her anxiety centers on Margaret's education.

An orphaned household held together by a servant's devotion gives this tale its heart. Janet nurses, earns, plans, and sacrifices in the approved manner of the improving story, yet the labor described is real labor. Scottish settings and Presbyterian conscience stiffen the sentiment. Readers get a period portrait of the faithful nurse as a type, drawn with admiration that modern eyes can share while questioning its terms.
23096-and-judas-iscariot-together-with-o:
Two thieves divide eternity in And Judas Iscariot, a set of evangelistic addresses published in 1906. One thief, the preacher says, let grace do its full work and won Christ's pardon. The other knew remorse but never repentance, and shut grace out. One became a mighty preacher. The other's crime still horrifies every reader.

Judas stands as the warning at the sermons' center, remorse mistaken for repentance. John Wilbur Chapman, the era's leading evangelist, built such addresses for mass revival meetings, and their structure shows it, contrast, urgency, appeal. The accompanying addresses work the same ground. Readers meet American revival preaching in its professional prime.
23135-history-of-circumcision-from-the-e:
Doctors form a class of their own in this History of Circumcision from the earliest times to the present. The operation, the author notes, went beyond the intellectual class. Doctors themselves form such a class across America, France, and England, he reports. Among medical families, he has personally found the practice observed by every male member, as a guard for health.

Peter Charles Remondino, the San Diego physician to whom the work is credited, surveys the rite across religions, climates, and centuries. His chapters mix anthropology, scripture, and medical argument in the confident manner of 1891. The book helped spread the era's medical case for the operation in America. Read now, it is a period document twice over, in its facts and in its certainties alike.
23144-the-war-trail-the-hunt-of-the-wild:
Thomas Mayne Reid rhapsodizes in The War Trail, the hunt of the wild horse. Reid greets Anahuac, old Mexico, like a lover returning. His fancy carries him back to its shores, its broad savannahs, and the shade of its corozo palms. Even his horse, he swears, neighs with joy at the scene.

Mexico's plains, mustangs, and war paths fill Reid's romance at full gallop. He climbs mountains of porphyry in the same breath, toward crags of quartz yielding white silver and yellow gold. Reid's prose was always half the adventure, purple, learned, and in love with the land it crossed. The hunt of the wild horse gives that prose its perfect subject.
23196-songs-for-a-little-house:
Christopher Morley published Songs for a Little House in 1917, a book of poems about home and daily life. One poem follows workers down Thirty-second Street at day's end. Their feet seem to chant homeward as they tramp, footsore and weary, yet stirred anew by the walk.

Nightfall makes up for the day: the ringing telephones stop, and golden train windows cast brightness on the snow. Morley writes plain city scenes with warmth and a light touch. Readers get short, musical poems that find comfort in streets, trains, and the small house waiting at the end of the day.
2358-the-after-house:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's After House is a sea mystery in which a yacht returns to port with its crew dead or missing and a young woman aboard who cannot explain what happened. The novel unfolds as a puzzle of murder at sea, with Rinehart's crisp narration keeping suspicion shifting among the survivors. The after house, the officers' quarters, gives the tale its title and its secrets.

Rinehart, already famous for The Circular Staircase, shows her gift for atmosphere and plot. The book moves fast and ends with a satisfying reveal. Mystery fans will enjoy this early example of her craft.
2568-trent-s-last-case:
E. C. Bentley dedicated this detective novel to G. K. Chesterton, in return for Chesterton's own tale of Thursday, and it made Philip Trent a famous name in crime fiction. Trent, an artist and amateur sleuth, is called to untangle the death of a rich financier, a case full of clues, lies, and false leads.

Bentley lets Trent reason brilliantly, then pulls the rug away: the detective's proud solution proves wrong. That twist made the book a landmark, teaching later writers that a clever detective can fail. Readers get a stylish puzzle, a sharp portrait of Edwardian wealth, and an ending that still surprises.
2772-the-country-house:
John Galsworthy sets this novel at Worsted Skeynes in October 1891, opening with a party and a railway station crowd. Mr. Horace Pendyce's omnibus, brougham, and luggage cart monopolize space, while his coachman's face monopolizes the station lantern's light.

The Pendyce family, its country house, and its tangled loves and debts drive a story of class, property, and passion. Galsworthy writes with his cool, observant irony about Edwardian England. The novel offers a rich portrait of a house and the people who cannot leave it. Worsted Skeynes station sets a whole world in motion.
3104-the-golden-house:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote The Golden House as a novel of New York society near midnight in a famous city studio. Guests gather believing the century's end is a time of license if not decadence, surprised to find themselves in bohemia, fluttering at the prospect of seeing an Oriental and ancient art unveiled. The hour, place, and anticipation give a titillating feeling of adventure and moral hazard bravely incurred.

The novel follows the Hendersons and their circle through art, money, and marriage, with later talk of the country becoming fashionable, syndicated, and a worry rather than a rest. Miss Tavish's visit to Bar Harbor and Lenox marks the social calendar. Warner's satire of wealth and taste remains graceful, if less famous than his travel writing.
3320-mohammed-ali-and-his-house:
Louise Mühlbach tells the life of Mohammed Ali in this historical novel, translated from the German by Chapman Coleman. Ali, the Albanian soldier who rose to rule Egypt, gives the book its center, and his house, his family and court, gives it its domestic drama. Mühlbach, a popular nineteenth-century novelist of courts and kings, writes history as intimate story.

The novel follows Ali from obscurity to power, through war, reform, and the rivalries of his household. Coleman, the translator, carries Mühlbach's brisk German into English. Readers who enjoy historical romance will find a ruler's life told from inside his family: ambition, affection, and statecraft sharing the same rooms.
3539-the-love-chase:
James Sheridan Knowles writes a comedy of courtship first performed at the Haymarket in 1837. The cast list names Sir William Fondlove, Waller in love with Lydia, Wildrake the sportsman, Trueworth, Neville, and a landlord called Chargewell. Waller, a fine spirit with a deep purse and easy strings, leads the town, while Wildrake, a country gentleman learned in dogs and horses, talks with great confidence.

The plot turns on rival suitors, disguises, and the chase after Lydia's hand, with lawyers, waiters, and friends adding confusion. Knowles writes in a lively, old fashioned comic style, full of wordplay and sudden entrances. The play suits readers interested in Victorian theater and in comedies where love must outwit money and pride.
3543-heartbreak-house:
George Bernard Shaw writes a play about cultured, leisured Europe just before the First World War, using a country house shaped like a ship as his stage. Shaw says Heartbreak House is not only the play's title but the condition of Europe itself, where clever people talked, flirted, and dreamed while the guns were being loaded. He links his play to Chekhov's studies of idle, charming people.

The characters include a retired sea captain, his daughters, and guests who drift through love affairs and arguments without acting. Shaw's preface notes that English audiences first called the play Russian, missing its English target. The play suits readers who enjoy Shaw's long, witty debates about a society sleepwalking toward war.
3746-the-judgment-house:
Gilbert Parker builds this novel around Jasmine, a woman whose beauty draws men into trouble, and the husband who cannot see what is plain to his friends. Chapters move from a jasmine flower and an underground world to Wales, the Appian Way, and the South African veld, where a powerful figure called the Baas bends events to his will. War cries, farm sieges, and letters from afar punctuate a domestic drama that keeps widening.

Parker writes with a popular novelist's pace, and his friends' anxious talk about Byng gives the story its ache. The book mixes romance, empire, and moral judgment in equal share, and its title points to the reckoning each character must face. Readers who like large Edwardian novels of love and power will find a full and stirring tale.
3755-common-sense:
Thomas Paine wrote this pamphlet in 1776 to persuade ordinary Americans that independence was not only right but plain common sense. He argues from the origin of government itself, then turns on monarchy and hereditary succession as absurd ways to choose a ruler. Later sections weigh the present state of American affairs and the continent's ability to stand alone, with Britain's distance and ignorance counted as proof that rule from London cannot work.

The prose is blunt and urgent, built for reading aloud in taverns and camps. Paine warns that Britain will try again after any defeat, and that petitions carried three thousand miles only waste months. The pamphlet helped turn a colonial quarrel into a revolution, and it still reads as a master class in political persuasion.
3802-the-lerouge-case:
Emile Gaboriau opens this founding detective novel in the village of La Jonchere, where five women report that the Widow Lerouge has not been seen for two days. Her cottage stands shut, door and shutters closed, and no knock wins an answer. The commissary at Bougival, tired of their importunities, sends for gendarmes and a locksmith to force the door. A crime comes to light in a quiet riverside place where crimes are rare.

From that forced entry the inquiry spreads through Paris and the provinces, as a dead woman's past yields secrets and suspects. Gaboriau builds his case step by step, with documents, alibis, and human frailty doing the work of detection. Readers who like the origins of the genre will find a patient, absorbing puzzle, written before fingerprints and laboratories took the stage.
4047-the-leavenworth-case:
Anna Katharine Green's detective novel opens with a great case: a murder in the Leavenworth house, probed by a coroner's inquest, expert testimony, and chains of circumstantial evidence. A lawyer narrator follows the clues, from facts and deductions to a sudden discovery.

Mary Leavenworth stands at the center of the mystery, watched by the detective Mr. Gryce and by readers who must weigh each side light. Green, a pioneer of the American detective tale, builds suspense from documents, motives, and careful reasoning. The novel suits readers who enjoy a classic whodunit where logic, not action, cracks the case.
4072-songs-before-sunrise:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Songs Before Sunrise opens an hour before dawn, with the speaker asking for a staff outside a hollow house that blind men fear. He lives on life withdrawn, feeling on sightless eyes the shadow of death that clothes Antigone.

Her living body lies dead in the poem's dark vision, if life is only blood and breath and sense. Swinburne's verse runs in long, musical waves, full of classical figures and republican hope. Readers who enjoy high Victorian lyric poetry will find a passionate, sometimes difficult book, written for the dawn of a freer age.
4099-the-angel-in-the-house:
Coventry Patmore's long poem The Angel in the House celebrates married love through preludes and cantos, including a Dean's canto on perfect love. Rare is still most noble found, Patmore writes, yet most noble still most incomplete, a sad law for lovers.

A postscript tells of violets, blue and white, enclosed by sisters who had won a wagered pair of gloves, and of Purcell's glee learned to sing by tomorrow night. The poem joins domestic detail to high ideal, praising a wife as angel of the home. Readers who like Victorian verse on love and marriage will find a famous, earnest classic.
4222-laperouse:
Ernest Scott wrote this life of the French navigator Jean-Francois de Galaup, comte de La Perouse, whose ships vanished in the Pacific after leaving Botany Bay in 1788. The chapters follow his family and youth, his naval career, a love story, the great voyage of exploration, and his stay at Botany Bay.

Scott also traces the mystery that followed, Captain Dillon's later discovery of wreckage, and the fame that kept La Perouse alive in Australian memory. The Sydney monument overlooking Botany Bay gives the book its starting point, and the narrative keeps returning to what that stone marks.
4337-power-through-repose:
Annie Payson Call wrote this book on the power that comes through repose, in a new edition with additions. Its motto, from Francois Delsarte, holds that personality binds while universality expands. Call argues that a body perfectly adjusted, well supplied with force, and free from waste becomes a perfect instrument of impression, experience, and expression.

The first chapter, on the guidance of the body, notes how much has been written on food, air, clothing, and development. What is lacking, Call says, is obedience to laws already known. Her remedy is restful attention rather than effort. The book founded a popular literature of relaxation, and it still reads as a gentle manual of self-care.
4339-nerves-and-common-sense:
Annie Payson Call, author of Power Through Repose, wrote this enlarged book of articles on nerves and common sense. Many pieces first appeared in the Ladies' Home Journal, whose editor Edward Bok supplied helpful titles. Call thanks him in her preface, and the contents show his hand in chapter names.

Chapters cover habit and nervous strain, how women can keep from being nervous, irritable husbands, the trying member of the family, and quiet versus chronic excitement. Later pieces treat working restfully, imaginary vacations, and how to be ill and get well. Call's advice is plain, domestic, and humane, aimed at daily life rather than theory.
434-the-circular-staircase:
Mary Roberts Rinehart sets this mystery in a rented country house where a middle-aged spinster finds murder on her hands. Rachel Innes, tired of town quiet, takes a furnished house for the summer and soon hears steps on a circular stair. A dead man, a missing nephew, and a bank scandal tangle round her.

Rinehart writes in Rachel's brisk, comic voice, mixing fright with domestic detail. Clues hide in cuff links, telegrams, and a hole in the wall. The novel, a landmark of the had-I-but-known school, still charms as a puzzle told by a heroine who refuses to faint.
4385-as-a-matter-of-course:
Annie Payson Call wrote this book in 1894 to help remove nervous irritants from everyday life. Such irritants, she argues in her preface, cause much physical disease and block usefulness and pleasure. Her chapters treat physical care, amusements, brain impressions, moods, tolerance, sympathy, and children, with a closing summary.

Call opens with a mountain image: a climber who knows the path takes it as a matter of course, and is free to enjoy the climb. Her counsel applies the same idea to nerves: do needful things without fuss, and drop the strain that comes from fussing. The book is a plain manual of restful living, in Call's gentle, practical voice.
4498-miscellaneous-prose:
George Meredith gathers several short prose pieces here, rather than a single novel or story. The set opens with his introduction to Thackeray's Four Georges, tracing Thackeray's life from Calcutta and Charterhouse to Cambridge and his early writing. It then adds brief essays called A Pause in the Strife, Concession to the Celt, and a sketch of Leslie Stephen.

Last come letters Meredith wrote to the Morning Post from the seat of war in Italy, reporting a campaign as a correspondent saw it. Together the pieces show Meredith as critic, commentator, and witness, not only as a novelist. Readers get a compact sample of his nonfiction voice: learned, witty, and quick to judge character, politics, and art.
450-susan-lenox-her-fall-and-rise:
David Graham Phillips follows Susan Lenox from a farm girlhood to city streets and back toward honor in this two-part novel, published in 1917. Orphaned and wronged, Susan is cast out, then drifts through theater, marriage, and the underworld of New York. Each fall costs her dearly, yet she keeps a stubborn sense of self.

Phillips writes with frank sympathy for a woman judged harshly by a double standard. Susan's rise, when it comes, rests on work, friends, and her own will, not rescue. The novel stands as a bold, humane study of a woman fighting for a decent life on her own terms.
4513-the-rainbow-and-the-rose:
E. Nesbit wrote this book of poems in 1905, dedicating it to Iris and Rosamund. Its contents divide into four parts, opening with the things that matter, the confession, work, the jilted lover, and the will to live. The beatific vision closes the first part, and mummy wheat, the beech tree, and songs follow.

Later poems include the veil of Maya, a song to Vera, the poet to his love, and the maiden's prayer. The magic flower, bridal eve, love and life, and songs from the Italian close the book, with a final part from the fullness of the heart. Nesbit's verse is lyrical and direct, on love, children, and the passing of time.
4618-words-for-the-wise:
T. S. Arthur published Words for the Wise in 1851, with a preface saying the title needs no explanation. May its lessons prove sufficient, he hopes, as warnings, incentives, and examples to hundreds and thousands of readers. The contents run from The Poor Debtor and The Sunday Christian. They go on to I Knew How It Would Be, Jacob Jones, and Starting a Newspaper, with an experience of Mr. Jones.

Later pieces include The Way of Transgressors, Just Going to Do It, and Making Haste to Be Rich. They go on to Let Her Pout It Out, A Fine Generous Fellow, Taking It for Granted, and Love and Law. The opening tale meets a rich merchant, Petron, who claims one honest man in the world, and a tailor, Moale, long under the weather. Readers get short, plain moral sketches, each with a warning or an incentive to carry into daily life.
4698-whitefoot-the-wood-mouse:
Thornton W. Burgess tells Whitefoot the Wood Mouse for young readers, opening with a happy winter in the Green Forest. Whitefoot, Burgess says, never lets past troubles spoil present happiness, and never borrows trouble from the future. Past things are past, and future things can wait until they happen, a wisdom Burgess thinks most human beings lack.

Whitefoot has more enemies to watch than any other little person in the forest, from Buster Bear downward, yet he stays happy whenever he has a chance. Chapters follow queer sights, Farmer Brown's boy, anxious days, a careless jump, a rescue, and two timid persons meeting. Readers get a gentle animal story about courage, watchfulness, and living in the present, easy to read aloud to children.
4745-at-the-villa-rose:
A. E. W. Mason sets At the Villa Rose in Savoy, opening with Mr. Ricardo's August habit of travelling to Aix-les-Bains. For five or six weeks he pretends to take the waters in the morning, and rides in his motor-car in the afternoon. He dines at the Cercle in the evening, and spends an hour or two in baccarat rooms at the Villa des Fleurs. Summer lightning, a cry for help, and Perrichet's story soon break that smooth life.

Chapters follow the villa itself, a salon, Helene Vauquier's evidence, and a startling discovery. A ship's captain, Madame Dauvray's motor-car, news from Geneva, an unopened letter, and an aluminium flask all enter the case. Celia's story, a seance, and explanations by Helene and by Hanaud close the mystery. Readers get a classic detective novel, elegant and twisty, with a French detective whose reasoning untangles a Riviera crime.
4775-theocritus-bion-and-moschus-rendere:
Andrew Lang, M.A., lately fellow of Merton College, Oxford, rendered Theocritus, Bion, and Moschus into English prose, with an introductory essay, published by Macmillan in 1889 and dedicated to Ernest Myers. Its contents open with Theocritus and His Age, then thirty idyls of Theocritus, from the first through the thirtieth, followed by his epigrams. Bion's six idyls and fragments follow, then nine idyls of Moschus.

A life of Theocritus, taken from Suidas, opens the discussion of the poet, calling him the Chian, while noting another Theocritus, son of Praxagoras and Philinna. Lang's essay places Theocritus in his age, among shepherds, fishermen, and town life of the Greek world, before the translations themselves begin. Theocritus's idyls, Bion's laments, and Moschus's shorter pieces together show Greek pastoral poetry in prose form, clear and readable. Readers get the three pastoral poets in one volume, with Lang's learned introduction.
4903-hilda-wade-a-woman-with-tenacity-of:
Grant Allen's Hilda Wade opens with a doctor narrator insisting that his subject's gift must be shown before it can be described. Hilda's talent is unique and extraordinary, and the episodes that follow illustrate it through her encounters with patients, colleagues, and the formidable Professor Sebastian at St. Nathaniel's Hospital.

Sebastian, fiery-eyed and past his prime, impresses the narrator with greatness of mind and force of character as much as with scientific fame. Allen builds the novel episode by episode, each testing Hilda's insight and resolve. Readers get a Victorian mystery of character, where a woman's perception becomes the story's driving power.
5089-boris-godunov-a-drama-in-verse:
Alexander Pushkin's Boris Godunov, a drama in verse, presents the Time of Troubles through a crowded cast. Varlaam is a wandering friar. Athanasius Pushkin is a friend of Shuisky. Feodor is the young son of Boris. Semyon Godunov serves as the tsar's secret agent. Prince Kurbsky, the Cossack Karela, Marina daughter of Mnishek, and Ksenia daughter of Boris share the stage.

At the story's center stands Dimitry the Pretender, formerly Gregory Otrepiev, claiming the throne against Boris's haunted reign. Pushkin's blank verse carries conspiracy, conscience, and crowd scenes with Shakespearean breadth. Readers get Russia's founding historical drama, compact, political, and still startling in its modernity.
5312-mother-goose-in-prose:
L. Frank Baum's Mother Goose in Prose, illustrated by Maxfield Parrish and published in New York in 1901, retells the nursery rhymes as short stories. An illustration of a little man with a little gun opens the book. Baum gives each rhyme a plot, a character, and a reason, turning verses children knew by heart into tales to read aloud.

Baum, soon to be famous for The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, writes here with humour and warmth for young readers. The book offers a charming doorway into Mother Goose, where the rhymes gain beginnings, middles, and ends. The illustrations remain among Parrish's most beloved work.
5625-flint-and-feather-collected-verse:
E. Pauline Johnson gathered her verse in Flint and Feather, a collection inscribed by gracious permission to the Duke of Connaught. A memoir introduction recalls that Johnson, on her deathbed, wished the writer of that introduction, living far away in the mother country, to write something about her. The poems themselves span her career as a Mohawk poet and performer.

Johnson's verse moves between Indigenous subjects, Canadian landscape, and lyric feeling, in the voice that made her famous on stage. Readers get the collected poems of a pioneering Indigenous Canadian writer, passionate, musical, and rooted in two cultures.
5660-mary-louise:
Edith Van Dyne wrote Mary Louise for young readers, introducing a heroine she calls very human and much like the reader herself. Van Dyne, author of the Aunt Jane's Nieces series and The Daring Twins, presents Mary Louise as really not a fiction character at all, but a girl readers might know. Her success, the preface says, rests largely on finding such a heroine.

The novel follows Mary Louise through family troubles, friendships, and adventures, with more volumes promised about the lovable girl. Van Dyne writes for girls with warmth and directness. Young readers get a friendly series opener, centered on a kind, brave, ordinary girl.
5795-the-secret-rose:
Yeats gathers mystical tales in The Secret Rose, dedicated to AE and opening with a dedication to the rose itself. Contents include The Crucifixion of the Outcast and Out of the Rose. The Wisdom of the King and The Heart of the Spring follow. The Curse of the Fires and of the Shadows and The Old Men of the Twilight complete the set. Each tale treats the rose as a symbol of spiritual beauty and hidden truth.

Readers enter Yeats's early world of saints, kings, outcasts, and twilight figures, where earthly life touches the eternal. The prose is ornate and musical, favoring vision over action, and the stories reward slow reading. Fans of symbolist fiction and Irish mysticism will find a defining Yeats collection, short enough to read in an evening and rich enough to revisit.
6324-the-story-of-a-white-rocking-horse:
One by one the lights go out in the toy department, shoppers and clerks leave, and only a small light guides the night watchman. Then a Calico Clown cries that they can have fun. A Lamb on Wheels warns that they must be sure no eyes watch, and the Bold Tin Soldier agrees, glad the store is empty. Laura Lee Hope's toys talk and move only when no one sees, and the White Rocking Horse sways at the centre of their night world.

Too large for the counter with clown, monkey, rabbit, and soldier, the horse and the lamb watch days pass and nights return, with kind boys preferred to one rude chap. The story belongs to Hope's Make Believe series, beside the Sawdust Doll and the Bold Tin Soldier. It is a gentle tale for children, where toys keep their society after closing time and kindness counts most.
6345-seven-maids-of-far-cathay-being-eng:
Bing Ding compiles English notes from a Chinese class book, written by seven Chinese girls of the graduating class at the Woman's Anglo-Chinese College of Neuchang. The college president set them a game for their last six months of course, their notes were read aloud, taken down by a stenographer, and arranged alphabetically. Friends asked for publication exactly as written, and the president permitted it.

The notes, illustrated by Ai Lang, show young writers practising English with charm and frankness, from dedications to a grandmother genius of geniuses to a night rescue on rocks. A boat comes near in darkness, one lantern flashes like an insect, and Miss Sterling's voice calls through the black night asking if all are safe. The book is a rare, direct record of Chinese schoolgirls writing in a new tongue.
6455-the-little-lady-of-the-big-house:
