Jack London's The Little Lady of the Big House opens in darkness, with Dick Forrest waking simply, without movement save eyes opening. Unlike most, he knows himself at once in time, place, and personality, taking up the interrupted tale of his days without effort. He is master of broad acres, fallen asleep after marking Road Town with a match and pressing off his electric reading lamp, near a sleepy fountain's ripple.

Far off, faint to a keen ear, comes the throaty bawl of King Polo, his champion Short Horn bull, thrice grand champion of all. Later, Paula, the little lady, introduces the house's sages with a warning. Dar Hyal abstains wholly, Theodore Malken gets poetically drunk on one cocktail, Aaron Hancock is an expert wine bibber, and Terrence McFane can put ninety nine men under the table. London writes a California ranch novel of wealth, love, and talk.
6618-poems-of-purpose:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathers poems of purpose in this 1919 London volume, from A Good Sport and A Son Speaks to Happiness and The Things That Count. War mothers, a superwoman, a bachelor to a married flirt, and a song of the road all find a place. The contents show a poet keen on conduct, courage, and the daily choices that shape a life.

Wilcox writes in plain, musical verse, with a moral that lands without preaching. Her poems suit reading aloud, one at a time, for a lift or a pause. Poems of Purpose is a warm, earnest set, full of the cheer and common sense that made Wilcox widely loved.
6679-the-old-stone-house:
Anne March, the pen name of Constance Fenimore Woolson, opens with Aunt Faith alone on a piazza on her birthday, the first of June. More than half a century lies behind her, and sad thoughts crowd in: a husband dead soon after marriage, brothers and sisters taken one by one. A psalm on sowing in tears and reaping in joy heads the book.

Five cousins, life at the old stone house, an editor's sanctum, a Fourth of July, a picnic, and a home-coming fill the chapters. March writes with gentle, domestic warmth, in the style of her day. The Old Stone House is a tender, old-fashioned tale of family, loss, and quiet hope.
7035-the-hero-of-hill-house:
Mabel Hale's Hero of Hill House follows Austin through home, strife, and faith, opening on a quiet late autumn evening at supper. The little farm family gathers round the table, but father's place stands vacant, since he has gone to town. Contents trace a stricken home, Austin and his father, humiliation, a runaway, wayside friends, and a captain's guest, with Uncle John again and Austin taking care of himself.

A revival, church membership, a battle of two wills, and seeking new pasture follow, with hay fields, six weeks of haying, and restlessness in between. Mother Hilman's opinion, troubled seas, and plans made for themselves lead to Austin and Amy, a shopping trip, and Harry Hill. The novel closes with a stormy season, a new home, and a parson's judgment.
7319-good-sense:
Baron d'Holbach's Good Sense, without God, or Freethoughts Opposed to Supernatural Ideas, comes here in an undated English translation of Le Bon Sens, its translator not stated. Its epigraph, borrowed from Bacon, argues that atheism leaves men to sense, philosophy, laws, and reputation as guides to virtue. Superstition, by contrast, dismounts them all and sets up an absolute monarchy in men's minds.

D'Holbach builds that case in short, plain arguments against priests, miracles, and fear, favouring reason and nature over revealed command. The Freethinker's Library edition keeps the tone bold and accessible, meant for readers, not scholars alone. The book remains a classic statement of Enlightenment unbelief.
7378-chantry-house:
Charlotte M. Yonge builds this Victorian family chronicle around a house and the brothers who belong to it. The narrator, pressed by the younger generation, sets down the story of Chantry House and his two elder brothers, working from diaries and letters. Memory reaches back to childhood, to a mother reading aloud, and to the family past that still shapes the present.

The tale unfolds through wills, discoveries, midnight chases, and reckonings, with a ghost of Lady Margaret haunting the margins. Yonge, a moral storyteller of the old school, ties the family's fortunes to duty, repentance, and restitution. The result is a long, leisurely novel of kinship and conscience, in which the house itself holds the family's history.
757-fifty-bab-ballads-much-sound-and-lit:
W. S. Gilbert gathered fifty of his Bab Ballads, comic verses written for the magazine Fun under the pen name Bab. The ballads tell absurd tales in brisk rhyme: policemen, sailors, ghosts, and lovers caught in topsy-turvy plots, all resolved with a wink. The subtitle, Much Sound and Little Sense, gives the game away.

Gilbert's humour is dry and precise, with a love of logic pushed to folly. These verses were the seedbed of his later operas with Sullivan, and many of their jokes and types reappear on stage. The book delights readers who enjoy nonsense verse with a sharp edge, where sense and sound swap places for fun.
805-this-side-of-paradise:
F. Scott Fitzgerald wrote this first novel about Amory Blaine, a handsome youth who grows from a romantic boy into a Princeton man and then into a disillusioned young adult. Book One, The Romantic Egotist, follows Amory's school and college days, his friendships, and his first loves, in prose that mixes narrative, verse, and drama.

Fitzgerald captures the restless mood of a generation after the Great War, with its hunger for beauty, wealth, and meaning. Amory's search ends not in triumph but in self-knowledge, hard won. The novel made Fitzgerald famous at twenty-three, and it remains the classic portrait of American youth on the edge of the Jazz Age.
8182-the-ghost-of-guir-house:
Charles Willing Beale published The Ghost of Guir House in 1897, opening with Mr Henley returning to his dingy little house in Twentieth Street. New York, where a servant hands him a letter the postman struggled to deliver. The letter bears several erased addresses and a note in the corner: Dead. Try Paul. Unfamiliar with the handwriting, Henley carries it upstairs, lights the gas, and begins to read, setting the mystery in motion.

The novel that follows links a New York present to a haunted house and a past that will not stay buried. Beale writes a Victorian ghost story of letters, identities, and old wrongs. For lovers of supernatural fiction, it is an atmospheric period piece, with a New York opening that leads into genuinely eerie territory.
835-the-grey-brethren-and-other-fragment:
Michael Fairless, author of The Roadmender, gathered these fragments in prose and verse in 1911. The Grey Brethren, the title piece, leads a set of short meditations, tales, and poems in the same gentle, devout spirit. Duckworth issued the volume, which reached a third impression in its first year.

Fairless writes of faith, nature, and the quiet duties of life, in prose that is simple and musical. The fragments are brief, meant to be read slowly and pondered. The book suits readers who loved The Roadmender, offering more of its author's calm wisdom in small, polished pieces.
8448-honor-edgeworth-or-ottawa-s-present:
Honor Edgeworth, or Ottawa's Present Tense, by Vera, was entered for copyright in Canada in 1882 by A. S. Woodburn of Ottawa. The preface promises an honest tale, plainly told, in Shakespeare's phrase, and the novel follows Honor Edgeworth through Ottawa society, in the capital's present tense, as the subtitle says.

Vera's novel belongs to early Canadian fiction, written when Ottawa was a young capital finding its social life. Readers get a period romance of manners, with Canadian settings and characters, from a writer using a pen name. The book interests students of Canadian literature, and readers who like Victorian domestic novels in a colonial setting.
8572-cord-and-creese:
James De Mille opens this adventure novel in Sydney, New South Wales, on the morning the ship Rival brings the English mail in July 1840. Crowds gather at the post office, street corners buzz with news from home, and a letter from beyond the sea sets the plot moving. Warehouses, offices, and the harbour give the opening a busy colonial port for a backdrop.

From that arrival, the story widens into the tangled fortunes, secrets, and sea-going ventures that the title hints at. De Mille, already known for The Dodge Club, writes at a brisk pace, letting letters, chance meetings, and sudden turns carry the reader forward. It is a good pick for anyone who likes old-fashioned adventure built on mystery, travel, and the long reach of a single piece of news.
8575-the-happy-days-of-the-empress-marie:
Imbert de Saint-Amand wrote The Happy Days of the Empress Marie Louise, translated by Thomas Sergeant Perry and illustrated. It follows the young empress from early years through 1809, the preliminaries of her wedding, and the betrothal. A religious difficulty, an ambassador extraordinary, the wedding at Vienna, the departure, the transfer, and the journey to France follow.

Marie Louise, Napoleon's second wife, lived her happy days before exile and loss, and Saint-Amand, a historian of Napoleon's women, tells them with court detail. Readers get a biography of a young empress at the height of empire, before its fall. The book suits readers of Napoleonic history, and of royal lives told through ceremony and anecdote.
8933-popular-tales-from-the-norse:
Sir George Webbe Dasent collects Popular Tales from the Norse, with an introductory essay on the origin and diffusion of popular tales. His introduction moves through origin, diffusion, Norse mythology, Norse popular tales, and conclusion, arguing that stories travel and change across peoples while keeping their bones. Notices to the first and second editions frame a book that helped create the study of folklore in English.

The tales themselves include True and Untrue, Why the Sea is Salt, the old dame and her hen, East o' the Sun and West o' the Moon. Boots who ate a match with the troll, Hacon Grizzlebeard, Boots who made the princess say that's a story, the twelve wild ducks. The giant who had no heart in his body. The fox as herdsman, the mastermaid, the cat on the Dovrefell, and the princess on the glass hill follow.
9221-the-old-manse-from-mosses-from-an-o:
Between two tall gate-posts of rough stone, Hawthorne first beheld the gray front of the old parsonage at Concord. The gate had fallen from its hinges at some unknown time. A year had passed since the last clergyman's funeral train left for the burying-ground. Grass overgrew the drive, grazed by vagrant cows and an old white horse.

Hawthorne, the new tenant, makes the reader acquainted with his abode, its avenue of black-ash trees, and its half-asleep shadows. The house seems barely of the material world. This preface remains a beloved opening to Mosses from an Old Manse, full of quiet wonder.
9224-buds-and-bird-voices-from-mosses-fr:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this spring sketch for Mosses from an Old Manse, as winter loosens its grip. Balmy Spring comes late, yet at last revives the moss on roof and walls of the old house. She peeps into his study window, and he throws it open to mix her genial breath with the stove's black cheer.

Thoughts and fancies of winter fly out into infinite space as the casement rises. Visions gay, grotesque, and sad give way to a fresh existence made of sunshine. The sketch is a joyful ode to spring, and to the mind waking with the year.
9225-monsieur-du-miroir-from-mosses-from:
No one in Hawthorne's circle has he studied more, yet known less, than the gentleman called Monsieur du Miroir. The narrator, a student of human nature, seeks who this figure really is, how he connects to himself, and what their joint interest may bring. He lays a few remarkable points before the public, hoping for a clue.

Readers soon guess the jest: Monsieur du Miroir is the man in the mirror, the self seen in glass. Hawthorne turns a fancy into grave reflection on identity. The sketch remains a witty, uncanny piece on the double every person carries.
9226-the-hall-of-fantasy-from-mosses-fro:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this sketch for Mosses from an Old Manse, on a hall he claims to visit at times. Its interior is a spacious hall with white marble floors, a lofty dome, and pillars like Moorish work from the Alhambra. Stained windows fill it with many-colored light, painting the floor with grotesque designs.

Inmates breathe a visionary air, as in a Gothic cathedral of the mind. Hawthorne uses the hall as an image of fancy itself, where famous shades meet. The sketch is a playful allegory of imagination, and a favorite among his shorter pieces.
9227-the-new-adam-and-eve-from-mosses-fr:
Suppose Father Miller's reading of prophecy came true, and the Day of Doom swept away all mankind. Hawthorne, in Mosses from an Old Manse, imagines a new Adam and Eve waking in a world emptied of artifice. We who live in an artificial system, he says, can hardly know how little in us is natural, and how much is man's perverted craft.

Art has become a stepmother, teaching us to scorn nature's wholesome gifts. Only fancy can loosen the fetters we call truth. The tale follows the pair through cities and fields, learning life anew. It remains a bold, strange fable on nature versus custom.
9228-the-christmas-banquet-from-mosses-f:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this tale for Mosses from an Old Manse, drawn from his unpublished Allegories of the Heart. Roderick, sitting with Rosina and a sculptor in a summer-house, unfolds a manuscript. He seeks to grasp a man who glides past him in life, a puzzle his sad experience cannot solve.

The sculptor urges him to propound the man, whom Roderick likens to marble carved with a mockery of intellect, yet lacking a heart. Hawthorne's allegory probes cold genius and feeling. The tale is dark, strange, and deeply characteristic of its author.
9229-the-intelligence-office-from-mosses:
A grave figure in mysterious spectacles sits at a desk in a city intelligence office, a pen behind his ear. Around the walls stick notices of things lost, wanted, or for sale, covering nearly all that human fancy has contrived. Tall buildings and blue and crimson show-bills shadow the room, while street noise beats outside.

Hawthorne, in Mosses from an Old Manse, uses the office as an emblem of human wanting itself. Seekers come and go, each with a loss or a wish. The sketch is a sly, humane satire on desire, and on the trade that promises to meet it.
9230-p-s-correspondence-from-mosses-from:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this tale for Mosses from an Old Manse, around his friend P., whose mind mixes past and present. P. has lost the thread of his life through long spells of disordered reason. Yet from a small whitewashed, iron-grated room he travels far in fancy, meeting persons long dead to all eyes but his.

Hawthorne calls this sport of imagination, half wilful and half forced by disease, vivid as a play on stage. The letters that follow show P.'s spectral meetings. The tale is tender and eerie, a study of madness as a kind of second sight.
9231-earth-s-holocaust-from-mosses-from-:
Once upon a time, whether past or to come matters little, the world grew overburdened with worn-out trumpery. Its people chose to rid themselves of it by a general bonfire on a broad western prairie, where no house stood in danger. Hawthorne journeys there, hoping the flames may reveal some moral truth hidden in mist.

The heap grows as old books, weapons, and vanities feed the fire, yet the heart's rubbish proves harder to burn. Hawthorne's fable asks what reform can truly purge. It remains a brilliant satire on progress, showing how little fire alone can change mankind.
9233-sketches-from-memory-from-mosses-fr:
Hawthorne's sketches from memory open in mid-September, on the road to the White Mountains. Since sunrise the party has climbed from Bartlett up the Saco valley, between mountain walls, toward old crystal hills whose brilliancy gleamed from afar. Height after height towers up, till clouds hang below the peaks.

Red pathways of slides scar the slopes, where avalanches of earth and trees left tracks ages cannot efface. Mountains stand behind, beside, and ahead. Hawthorne's prose turns travel into poetry. The sketches remain a classic of American mountain writing, observant and grand.
9235-a-virtuoso-s-collection-from-mosses:
With a leisure hour to spare, Hawthorne steps into a new museum, drawn by a small sign: To be seen here, a virtuoso's collection. Up a sombre stair he pays half a dollar to a doorkeeper in a faded great-coat, whose marked face promises something out of the ordinary way. Inside waits a cabinet of wonders.

The collection holds relics of history and fable, each with a tale attached, from famous folk and fabled beasts. Hawthorne turns the museum into a meditation on fame and curiosity. The sketch is a delightful cabinet piece, witty and quietly melancholy.
9410-helen-of-the-old-house:
Harold Bell Wright, a best-selling American novelist, published Helen of the Old House in 1921. The novel sets a mill town's labor strife beside two women both named Helen, and an old house that binds their fates. A figure called the Interpreter speaks for a moral view of work and wealth. The book moves from a hut on a cliff to the mill, the strike, and the town's reckoning.

As the strike builds, managers, workers, and town folk clash over wages, power, and fair dealing. Wright pleads for a middle path: honest work, fair pay, and care for the common good. The prose is earnest and plain, aimed at a wide crowd. A reader gets a popular 1920s take on capital and labor, told as a human story, not a tract.
9606-a-little-book-of-western-verse:
Eugene Field wrote A Little Book of Western Verse in 1889, poems of the American West and of home. Field dedicated the book to Mary Field French, who fostered him as a child after his mother's death. His dedication thanks her patient heart and asks her kind eye for his faults. The poems that follow mix memory, humor, and tenderness.

Verses recall loved ones passed away, western scenes, and small home joys, in Field's easy, musical style. A Memory opens the run, on loss and the ache of absence. A reader gets a fond, old-style book of verse, where the West meets the hearth, and a poet's gratitude runs through every line.
982-the-book-of-nonsense:
Edward Lear wrote this Book of Nonsense, a set of drawings and verses for children, dedicated to the great-grandchildren, grand-nephews, and grand-nieces of Edward, thirteenth Earl of Derby. The opening limerick tells of an Old Derry down Derry, who loved to see little folks merry and made them a book at which they shook with laughter.

Lear's limericks, with their odd folk and places, and his drawings to match, invented a whole genre of nonsense verse. The book, made for the Derby children, has delighted generations since. It remains a classic of children's literature, where silliness is an art and every page invites a laugh.
9889-songs-and-other-verse:
This ninth volume of Eugene Field's collected writings gathers his songs and shorter poems. Field, a Chicago journalist and poet, wrote verses meant to be read aloud, full of children, home, and everyday feeling.

Among the pieces are a dream-ship ballad, a song for a mother's grave, love songs after Heine, and light tales of tailors and journalists. The tone shifts from tender to playful without losing its musical ease. Readers who like poetry that sings rather than puzzles will find Field at his most charming here, in short pieces that reward reading aloud.
9979-de-libris-prose-and-verse:
Austin Dobson's 1908 book of prose and verse takes books and their associations as its subject, as its title, De Libris, promises. Dobson addresses the reader as lector benevole, the kindly reader of old, and admits he cannot make anyone read the pages that follow.

Inside are essays and poems on books, authors, and the pleasures of collecting, in Dobson's polished, eighteenth-century manner. Published by Macmillan in London, the book suits lovers of old volumes and quiet libraries. Readers who enjoy bibliophily will find wit, learning, and affection on every page.
9989-bees-in-amber-a-little-book-of-thou:
John Oxenham's 1913 little book of thoughtful verse opens with a credo and moves through the year's days, a philosopher's garden, and flowers of the dust. Oxenham, a popular devotional poet, writes short poems meant to be pondered, not merely admired.

Later pieces follow the pilgrim way, the potter and the pruner at their work, whirring wheels, the bells of Ys, and a little poem of life. The tone is earnest, hopeful, and plain. Readers looking for brief, reflective poetry for quiet moments will find these verses easy to carry and return to.
a-legend-of-montrose:
Walter Scott set his novel during the Scottish civil wars of the 1640s, when the Marquis of Montrose raised the Highlands for the King. Scott's introduction says the tale centers on the sad fate of young Lord Kilpont and on James Stewart of Ardvoirlich, the man whose hand struck him down. Feuds between great families open the story.

The main text follows soldiers and Highlanders through camps and marches, with the talkative soldier Dugald Dalgetty among its best-loved figures. Appendices add Clan Alpin's Vow and The Children of the Mist, with Scott's notes. Battles, loyalty, and clan hatred drive a compact, stirring piece of Scottish history in fiction.
an-anthology-of-australian-verse:
Bertram Stevens edited this gathering of Australian poets, writing the introduction himself. The contents begin with William Charles Wentworth and Charles Harpur, early voices of the colony. They run through Sir Henry Parkes and Rolf Boldrewood. They end with Adam Lindsay Gordon, whose Sick Stock-rider became a bush classic. Henry Kendall's Leaves from Australian Forests and Songs from the Mountains appear in force.

The poems sing of drought, floods, horses, shearing sheds, and the strange light of the bush, beside love lyrics and city verse. Stevens aimed to show that a young country had already made a literature. The anthology served for years as the standard doorway into Australian poetry.
as-a-matter-of-course:
Annie Payson Call published As a Matter of Course in 1894 as a handbook for calming the nerves. Call, already known for Power Through Repose, aims to remove nervous irritants from daily life. Her preface says such irritants cause disease and spoil usefulness and pleasure. The governing image is a stone in the traveller's path.

Call argues that small obstacles should be stepped over as a matter of course, without fretting. Chapters treat physical care, amusements, brain impressions, and the triviality of trivialities. Others handle moods, tolerance, sympathy, children, and illness. She distinguishes sentiment from sentimentality near the close. The book belongs to the New Thought movement, which taught mental habits as a path to health, and it still reads as gentle, practical psychology.
at-the-villa-rose:
A. E. W. Mason's At the Villa Rose is a detective novel of the French Riviera and Geneva. Mr. Ricardo, a rich widower approaching fifty, takes his annual cure at Aix-les-Bains. He pretends to take the waters and plays baccarat at the Villa des Fleurs. Inspector Hanaud of the Paris Sûreté is holidaying nearby.

A cry for help draws Ricardo into the murder of Madame Dauvray at her villa. Her companion Celia disappears, and her maid Hélène Vauquier gives evidence. Chapters pursue an unopened letter, an aluminium flask, and a séance. Hanaud explains at the close, gathering the threads in Geneva and Aix. Mason writes polished fair-play detection, with Ricardo as the bewildered amateur beside the great detective. The novel helped define the country-house mystery between the wars of crime fiction.
boris-godunov-a-drama-in-verse:
Alexander Pushkin's Boris Godunov, rendered into English verse by Alfred Hayes, dramatizes Russia's time of troubles. The cast list names Boris, afterwards Tsar, with Princes Shuisky and Vorotinsky at his court. Father Pimen, an old monk and chronicler, keeps the record. Gregory Otrepiev, a young monk, will become the Pretender.

The play opens in the Kremlin palace in February 1598, as Boris hesitates to accept the crown. Pimen's cell reveals the murder of the Tsarevich Dimitry, the secret on which Boris's reign is built. Gregory flees to Poland, takes Dimitry's name, and wins Marina Mnishek's ambition. Armies, taverns, and battlefields carry the short scenes onward. Pushkin wrote in Shakespeare's chronicle manner, letting the people themselves judge their tsar. It remains Russia's great historical drama.
brentano-die-drei-nusse:
Three nuts, each holding a wonder and a test, drive Brentano's fairy tale Die drei Nuesse, given here in German. The hero's fortune turns on what the nuts conceal and when he dares to open them. Folk tradition supplies the bones; Brentano's Romantic richness supplies the flesh.

Small as the tale is, it shows a master working magic in the briefest compass. Wishes, dangers, and rewards arrive in classic fairy-tale rhythm. The German text lets readers savor his musical prose directly. Brentano could fill a paragraph with more enchantment than others manage in a chapter. The story makes a perfect short sample of his art for new readers.
bulchevy-s-book-of-english-verse:
Arthur Quiller-Couch edited this great anthology of English verse, issued here under a generic title because the Oxford name was a trademark. Quiller-Couch arranged the poems by author in time order, beginning with anonymous songs from about 1250. Chaucer and Hoccleve appear early; the book runs on to poets born in the later nineteenth century.

His preface explains the choices: the best poems, whole where possible, in the order English poetry grew. Ballads, lyrics, odes, and dramatic verse stand side by side. Generations of readers met English poetry through this single shelf-sized volume. It works still as a map of the tradition, generous in range and firm in taste.
captain-fracasse:
Theophile Gautier's Captain Fracasse follows the ruined young Baron de Sigognac, who leaves his decaying Castle Misery with a traveling theater troupe. The contents promise the Chariot of Thespis, brigands, a snowstorm, and the Blue Sun inn. Sigognac takes the stage name Captain Fracasse, a braggart soldier's part.

He falls for the actress Isabella while the Duke of Vallombreuse schemes to steal her, setting duels, abductions, and melees in motion. Gautier, who adored the theater, fills seventeenth-century France with players, swordsmen, and the gypsy girl Chiquita. The baron's first victory gives him confidence his enemy must now reckon with. Gautier's swashbuckler remains a French classic of romantic adventure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-and-sch:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Clonmacnoise describes the abbey and school on the Shannon, halfway between Athlone and Banagher, as the most remarkable of Erin's ancient schools. Its founder, St. Ciaran, called Son of the Carpenter, chose a bleak region as better suited to followers of the Cross than the rich plains nearby.

Born at Fuerty in 512 and schooled by St. Finnian at Clonard, Ciaran joined the saintly youths later known as the Twelve Apostles of Erin. Finnian trusted the young Ciaran to teach and give out prayers in his absence, and would gladly have resigned his chair to keep him. The entry follows Ciaran's foundation and the school's fame among Ireland's monastic centres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-melr:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Melrose describes an abbey in Roxburghshire, founded in 1136 by King David the First as Scotland's earliest Cistercian monastery. Its first community came from Rievaulx, and St. Mary's Abbey stood complete within ten years in a wide valley south of the Tweed.

English incursions ravaged Melrose repeatedly: Edward the Second's soldiers desecrated, pillaged and burned the church, and Richard the Second laid waste the country and fired the abbey in 1385. Through Robert the Bruce's generosity a statelier church began in 1326, cruciform and two hundred and fifty feet long, famed for the fairy lightness of its carvings and window tracery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-newh:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Newhouse describes the first Premonstratensian abbey in England, near Brockelsby in Lincolnshire, founded in 1143 by Peter de Gousel. Peter acted with his lord Hugh de Bayeux's consent and Bishop Alexander of Lincoln's approbation, bringing a colony from Liegues Abbey near Calais under Abbot Henry.

William, Earl of Lincoln, hospitably received the White Canons and confirmed the gifts to Gelro, Newhouse's first abbot. Raised for Our Lady and St. Martial of Limoges, Newhouse became parent house to eleven English Premonstratensian houses. Granted to Charles, Duke of Suffolk, in Henry the Eighth's thirtieth year, only parts of its old foundations remain, and twenty-six abbots' names are known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-fa:
The name Alessandro Farnese belongs to two cardinals, and this entry treats the younger. He was the son of Pier Luigi Farnese, first Duke of Parma, born in October 1520 and dead at Rome in February 1589. While a student at Bologna, he was made administrator of Parma in 1534. His uncle Paul III created him Cardinal-Deacon of Sant' Angelo that December and conferred offices and benefices on him.

Farnese was zealous for the poor and served the popes on legations and embassies, including a 1539 mission to Charles V and a 1545 embassy on the council. He accompanied papal troops against the Smalkald League in 1546 and stood as a candidate for the papacy in 1580. A promoter of the Tridentine reforms and a patron of literature, science, and art, he backed the architect Vignola for the Gesù in Rome and the palace at Caprarola. He was buried before the high altar of the Gesù.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-of-repo:
The altar of repose, sometimes called sepulchre or tomb, more often repository, holds the Sacred Host consecrated at Holy Thursday Mass until Good Friday's Mass of the Presanctified. It must stand in the church, other than the altar where Mass is celebrated. Two hosts are consecrated on Holy Thursday. After the first is consumed, the second rests in a chalice covered with pall and inverted paten, under a white veil tied with ribbon, on the corporal until Mass ends.

The host is then borne in solemn procession to that altar of repose. It is kept in the tabernacle or an urn above the altar. Churches vie to adorn these altars and chapels with rich hangings, flowers, and lights, and Holy Thursday becomes a day of exceptional devotion. No mention of altar and procession appears before the late fifteenth century, earlier reservation having served Communion distribution, not the next day's service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-vase:
The Caeremoniale Episcoporum sanctions flowers between the candlesticks as certainly appropriate altar ornaments. Altar vases hold flowers decorating the altar, natural or artificial blooms set between the candlesticks as fitting ornaments for worship. Cut flowers, leaves, and ferns are meant here, rather than soil-potted plants, though potted plants may adorn the sanctuary around the altar.

Artificial flowers must use superior material and copy nature's variations faithfully and with some accuracy. Paper, cheap muslin, calico, and other inferior stuffs, and old or soiled flowers, are never allowed on the altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Funen, Langeland, Taasinge, Laaland, Falster, Als, and Aero made up Odense. It was founded before 988, split off from Schleswig, and its first Odense church honoured Saint Mary. Othinkar Hvide the Elder preached in Funen. Reginbert, an Englishman, is the first bishop known with certainty. Canterbury's Archbishop Alnoth consecrated him in 1020 or 1022, and King Canute the Great sent him to Denmark.

After Eilbert of Bremen, Roskilde held the vacant see until Hubald, an English Benedictine, took it as bishop in 1086. In that year King Saint Canute was murdered in Odense's Saint Alban church. Miracles and poor harvests after the murder led to his canonization. Hubald moved his relics in 1101 to the new church of Our Lady and Saint Alban. Twelve Evesham monks, sent in 1100, served the new Saint Canute cathedral and formed its chapter. Odense later counted among Denmark's richest bishoprics. Its cathedral crypt holds Canute and his brother Benedict.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anise:
Since Wyclif, English versions have rendered anethon in Matthew 23:23 as anise, but that rendering is not accurate. Dill, anethum graveolens, is anethon's exact equivalent, while anise is pimpinella anisum. The mistake matters little, since both plants belong to the parsley family and share many properties. Dill grows as an annual, with striated stems one to one and a half feet high, pinnate leaves, and yellow flowers. Jews used it as a condiment.

Rabbinic literature mentions it several times, especially over tithes. Beside the articles named in the Mosaic Law, the Rabbis over time brought many other objects under tithe, extending it to every edible product that could be preserved. A single Gospel word thus opens a study of translation, botany, and Jewish tithe practice, showing how a familiar rendering can hide a different plant and a wider custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apocalypse:
Apocalypse, from a Greek verb meaning to reveal, is the name attached to the last book of the Bible, also called the Book of Revelation. Though Christian, it belongs to a class of writing on end times much in vogue among Jews of the first century before and following Christ. Its author calls himself John, writing to seven churches in Asia from the island of Patmos. Tradition identifies this seer as John the Apostle, son of Zebedee, the disciple Jesus loved.

By the end of the second century the principal churches accepted the work as genuinely John's. Melito of Sardis, one of the seven churches, wrote a commentary on it. Irenaeus in Gaul firmly held its divine and apostolic authority, and African witnesses agreed. The article then treats authenticity and interpretation, giving readers the Catholic case for a book of visions that closes the New Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-appeal-as-fro:
Appeal as from an abuse, in French appel comme d'abus, began as a recourse to the civil court against a church court seizing civil jurisdiction. Likewise it was a recourse to the church court against a civil court seizing church jurisdiction. So defined, it was in itself legitimate, since its object was to guard the rights of state and church alike. An abuse meant an act by either side, without due authority, beyond its own ordinary and natural bounds.

Church canons did not bar recourse to civil authority when a church judge invaded civil ground. That reciprocity let church authority repel a lay judge's invasion of church rights with the same weapons. Recourse to the supreme civil ruler was likewise not deemed wrong when a church court overstepped. The entry traces a device meant to keep two powers in their lanes, before it hardened into a tool of state control.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apse:
An apse, from Latin apsis and Greek apsis, an arch, is the semicircular or polygonal end given to a church's choir or aisles. Sometimes it is given to transepts and nave. In church architecture it generally marks the part where clergy sit or the altar stands, named for its usual dome or vault. The word also covers a canopy over an altar, a dome, or a semicircular recess vaulted with a half dome.

The apse is always solid below, though usually pierced by windows above. A chevet is an apse enclosed by a colonnade on the ground floor, opening into an aisle that in turn opens into three or more apse chapels. Sometimes a smaller semicircle sprouts from a simple one, as at Canterbury. The entry is a lexicon of one shape and its many church uses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archdiocese: Archdiocese, from Greek archidioikesis, does not name an ecclesiastical province as a whole. It names only the province's diocese which is the archbishop's own, over which he holds direct and exclusive jurisdiction. The entry distinguishes the archbishop's home diocese from the wider province he presides over, and cites Ferraris, Wernz, Smith, Phillips, and other canon law authorities for the definition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-be:
Bernard of Besse, a Franciscan chronicler of Aquitaine, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birth date is uncertain, and he served as secretary to St. Bonaventure, the order's great theologian. After Bonaventure's death he took up the pen, as he put it, to gather the ears dropped from his master's sheaf.

His Book in Praise of Blessed Francis, written about 1280, gathers early legends and gives precious notes on Francis's companions and the founding of the three Franciscan orders. It alone among thirteenth-century documents lists the first lives of Francis. The entry presents a modest secretary preserving a founder's memory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-everald-ha:
Blessed Everald Hanse, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Northamptonshire and educated at Cambridge, he held a good parish living until his brother William, ordained in 1579, pressed him toward conversion. A sharp illness turned him inward, and he went to Reims in 1580 for ordination.

His English ministry proved very short. Visiting Catholic prisoners in the Marshalsea in disguise in July 1581, his foreign-made shoes betrayed him to the keeper, and examination exposed his priesthood. With no law yet against priests as such, prosecutors stretched treason law to condemn him. He was executed on 31 July 1581.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-frances-d-:
Blessed Frances d'Amboise, Duchess of Brittany and later Carmelite nun, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1427, daughter of Louis d'Amboise, she was betrothed at four to Peter, second son of Duke John V, and married at fifteen. A morose husband ill-treated her at first, but her gentleness changed his heart.

After his succession in 1450, her influence widened into works of charity and good government across Brittany. Widowed, she entered the Carmelites and died at Nantes in 1485, having founded a Carmelite house there. The entry presents a duchess whose patience reformed a court and then a convent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-woo: Blessed Thomas Woodhouse, a martyr, suffered at Tyburn on 19 June 1573. He took orders under Queen Mary, served briefly as a Lincolnshire rector, and tutored privately in Wales in 1560. Arrested while saying Mass in 1561, he spent the rest of his life in custody. He said Mass in secret daily and recited his Office. A letter to Lord Burghley in 1572, urging reconciliation, brought his execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boise:
Boise, the Idaho diocese created by Leo XIII in 1893, covers the whole state, 84,290 square miles. Catholic work began in 1842 with a Jesuit mission to the Coeur d'Alene Indians, whose first church used wooden pegs instead of nails. Secular priests reached the Boise Basin miners in 1863 and built Idaho's first churches for white settlers within six months.

Idaho became a vicariate apostolic in 1868 under Louis Lootens, consecrated at San Francisco. He reached Idaho in January 1869, and the first Boise church rose in 1870, only to burn soon after dedication. His successor Alphonsus Glorieux, consecrated in 1885, found about 2,500 Catholics and ten churches served by two secular and several Jesuit priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burse:
A burse is the flat case that carries the folded corporal, the linen cloth used at the altar, to and from Mass. In Roman form it is two pieces of stiff card, about ten inches square, joined on three sides and open on the fourth to take the cloth. Its outer side matches the vestments in use, while the inside is lined with linen or silk.

The burse is fairly recent. Once the corporal shrank to its present small size, it was carried in the missal or in a box or bag. That holder at last took this flat form. A Mainz chronicle of 1140 to 1251 mentions a precious corporal case, and Saint Charles Borromeo describes a small corporal bag apart from the storage case. Between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries the burse spread, and by 1692 Mass without one was everywhere unlawful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camaldolese:
The Camaldolese are hermits and cenobites in one order, founded by Saint Romuald early in the eleventh century. About 1012, after founding or reforming nearly a hundred houses, Romuald reached the diocese of Arezzo. There Count Maldolus, who had dreamed of white-clad monks climbing a ladder to heaven, gave him the field that became Camaldoli. A villa below became Fonte Buono, serving as infirmary, guest-house, and bursary so the hermits stayed free of worldly business.

For six centuries the order grew as one body under the Holy Hermitage. It then split into five congregations: the Holy Hermitage, San Michele di Murano, Monte Corona, Turin, and Notre-Dame de Consolation. By 1907 three congregations remained, with houses chiefly in Italy, plus Bielany in Poland and Nuova Camaldoli in Brazil. The hermits at Camaldoli and the cenobites at Fonte Buono still stand as models of austerity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cause:
Cause, from the Greek aitia and Latin causa, is understood as that which gives existence to a thing, produces a result, or accounts for its origin. The article warns that cause, being transcendental, admits no strict logical definition. It then surveys the idea across philosophy, science, and law. It opens with the Pre-Socratics, Plato, and Aristotle. Their thought shaped every later account.

The scholastic analysis follows, dividing causation into material, formal, efficient, and final causes. The survey continues through Bacon, Descartes, Hume, Reid, and Kant, then Hegel and Schopenhauer. Later sections treat cause in science, in common sense, and in law. In law, a cause of action means an enforceable claim that may lapse with time or await a legal condition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chapter-house:
A chapter house stands beside a monastery or cathedral and holds the chapter's meetings. In monasteries it served each day after Prime, and at times after Terce, for reading the Martyrology and Necrology, correcting faults, and assigning the day's tasks. It also hosted the superior's exhortation and the evening Collation before Complin. Secular canons used it for similar purposes and for the formal business of the body corporate.

The chapter house appears in neither St. Benedict, who died in 543, nor the ancient plan of St. Gall drawn up in 820; monks then probably met for chapter in a cloister walk near the church. A separate building soon proved necessary, and the chapter house is named in Aachen council statutes of 816. Its shape varied from rectangular to apsidal, circular, or polygonal, with the polygonal form, carefully designed and richly ornamented, a triumph of thirteenth-century England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-const:
Charles Constantine Pise was a priest, poet, and prose writer born at Annapolis in 1801 and dead at Brooklyn in 1866. Educated at Georgetown College and for a time a Jesuit, he taught rhetoric at Emmitsburg's Mount St. Mary's College, where his pupils included the future Archbishop of New York, John Hughes. Ordained in 1825, he served at Baltimore cathedral and at St. Patrick's in Washington. There he was elected Senate chaplain in 1832, the only Catholic priest yet appointed to that office.

He was a friend of President Tyler. He became pastor of St. Peter's in New York in 1848. From 1849 until his death he served St. Charles Borromeo's in Brooklyn. His books include a five-volume History of the Catholic Church, Father Rowland, Alethia, St. Ignatius and His First Companions, and Christianity and the Church. His poem Clara and his drama Montezuma were never published. He also composed Latin verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-de-la:
Charles de La Fosse was a painter born at Paris in 1636 and dead there in 1716, buried in the church of Saint Eustache. Seventh of sixteen children of a jeweller and Marguerite Langlois, he trained under François Chauveau and then in Lebrun's studio. He later decorated the Tuileries. On 23 June 1673 he joined the academy, and five months later he married Elizabeth Beguin at Saint Sulpice.

Lord Montagu, ambassador to Paris in 1688, admired his work so much that he called him to England to decorate Montagu House. William III begged him to stay and decorate Hampton Court, but the architect Mansart recalled him to Paris for the dome of the Invalides. The Louvre's Galerie d'Apollon ceiling is also his, and he did much work at Versailles, including the Salle de Diane and the chapel roof.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charterhouse:
An entry on the charterhouse, the English name for a Carthusian house, from Chartreux near Grenoble, where St. Bruno founded the first house. Just as such houses are called cartuja in Spain and certosa in Italy, so Chartreux was corrupted in England into charterhouse. Henry II founded the first English house at Witham in Somerset in 1181, and Henry V founded the last, Sheen in Surrey, in 1414.

Other houses stood at Hinton, Beauvale, Coventry, Hull, and Mountgrace, but the most famous was the London charterhouse, founded in 1371 by Sir Walter Manny. Its prior, Blessed John Houghton, was put to death in 1535, and Henry VIII broke up its community. The entry also lays out the common plan of Carthusian houses: two courtyards, cells for choir monks and lay brothers, and a chapter house and refectory. The church has no aisles, and a great cloister gives onto each monk's cell and garden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chronicle-of-:
An entry on the Chronicle of Melrose, a monastic history opening in 735 and ending abruptly in 1270. It rests solely on the Cottonian manuscript Faustina B. the British Museum's nine, the only ancient copy, from which all others are transcripts. Its authors are unknown, but its language proves it was written in Melrose Abbey, and its shifting hands show monks of successive periods at work.

The first part, to about 1140, compiles the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and histories by Simeon of Durham and Hoveden, and must be used with caution. The second part, from about 1140 to 1270, ranks among the most credible sources of its age, since its entries are largely original and generally contemporary. The manuscript, likely carried off at the Reformation, was edited by Stevenson for the Bannatyne Club in 1835. Melrose also left hundreds of charters from David the First to Bruce, edited by Cosmo Innes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civita-castel:
Civita Castellana, a town on the Treia in Rome province, was built on the ruins of ancient Falerii, capital of the Falisci. That Latin tribe warred often with Rome until Camillus subdued it in 394 before Christ, though it rose again in 356 and during the Samnite War. Digging there has revealed much Faliscan civilisation. Alexander the Third died and was buried at Civita Castellana, and in 1798 the Austrians under Mack were beaten there by the French general Macdonald.

The first known bishop, Crescentius, found the relics of Martianus and Johannes in 998. In 1437 the diocese united with Orte, the ancient Horta on a travertine hill north of Rome, near the newly found catacombs of Saint Eutychius. Gallese joined Civita Castellana in 1252, was restored in 1562, and was suppressed again in 1573. The diocese, directly subject to the Holy See, counts 40,200 people, twenty-nine parishes, and over two hundred churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
The Councils of Anse, several medieval synods in a French town near Lyons, open in 994 with a decree for Sunday's vigil: no servile labour after three o'clock on Saturday afternoon. The 1025 council settled a clash between Cluny's monks and the Bishop of Macon over ordinations. Ancient canons read at the meeting subjected abbots and monks to their own bishop.

Later meetings pursued Gregory VII's reforms in 1076, heard Lyons' archbishop seek a Jerusalem journey subsidy in 1100 before Anselm of Canterbury, and decreed on faith and investitures in 1112. The 1025 ruling forced Vienne's archbishop to apologise to Macon, a small scene of medieval jurisdiction in action.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocese:
A diocese is the territory and churches subject to a bishop. The word began in Greek as the management of a household, then meant government in general. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry shows how Roman law used it for a district tied to a city. Since the Christian bishop usually lived in such a city, his territory took the same civil name.

Later sections treat the making, splitting, joining, and ending of dioceses, their different ranks, and how they are run. The bishop rules as a whole, yet must keep the general laws of the Church, and some sees stand free of any archbishop, answering straight to Rome. The entry closes with a survey of the diocesan system across the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dom-francois-:
Dom Francois Armand Gervaise was a Discalced Carmelite born at Paris in 1660. After brilliant studies he joined the order and served as prior of a convent. Bossuet noticed him there as a single man combining fervent religious life, learned writing, and eloquent speech. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how hunger for a stricter life took him to La Trappe in 1695. There he became the favored disciple of the Abbe de Rance.

On the death of Rance's first successor, the king, urged by Bossuet, named Gervaise as second successor. His rule brought strife, and he was at last banished by royal order to the monastery of the Reclus, where he died in 1761. To the end he kept the full rigor of the Trappist life he had embraced.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enemond-masse:
Enemond Masse was one of the first Jesuits sent to New France, born at Lyons in 1574 and dead at Sillery in 1646. He sailed to Acadia with Father Biard, and when no good could be done there, the two set up a new mission at what is now Bar Harbor in Maine. English attackers soon destroyed it, setting Masse adrift at sea in an open boat.

He reached a French ship and came home, only to sail again for Canada in 1625, staying until the fall of Quebec. A third voyage in 1632 brought him back for good, but age kept him from labouring among the native peoples. He lived mostly at Sillery, which he built as a reserve for converted Indians, and a monument now stands there on the site of the old Jesuit church above Quebec.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-d-ai:
Francois d'Aix de la Chaise, also called Chaize, was born at the Aix mansion in Forez on 25 August 1624 and died at Paris on 20 January 1709. He was confessor to Louis XIV for thirty-four years.

He is often blamed for conniving at the king's liaison with Madame de Montespan and advising the revocation of the Edict of Nantes with violent suppression of Protestants. The entry corrects the record. La Chaise used all his influence, with Madame de Maintenon, to end the Montespan liaison. After Queen Maria Theresa's death in 1683 he advised the king's marriage to Maintenon, which changed court life for the better. How far he backed the revocation is unknown, but the charge that he urged violence is baseless and clashes with his admitted mildness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-d-ambo:
George d'Amboise, a French cardinal, archbishop, and statesman born in 1460, ruled France beside Louis XII for a dozen years. Named Bishop of Montauban at fourteen, he took office at twenty-four and became Archbishop of Rouen in 1493. When his ally the Duke of Orléans took the throne as Louis XII in 1498, d'Amboise became prime minister and a cardinal the same year.

At home d'Amboise cut taxes a tenth, set finances in order, and reformed law and courts. Abroad he pushed Louis toward Milan. As a churchman he fared worse, chasing the papacy at Alexander VI's death and polling third with thirteen votes, then backing Pius III and flirting with schism against Julius II. Julius still made him legate for all France, an office he held until his death at Lyons in 1510.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-gervas:
George Gervase, a priest and martyr born in Suffolk in 1571, died at Tyburn for the priesthood alone. Orphaned young, he was kidnapped by pirates and held beyond the seas over twelve years, losing his religion in captivity. Back in England he found his brother Henry exiled in Flanders for the faith, followed him there, and was reconciled to the Church. He entered Douai's English College in 1595 and was ordained in 1603.

Gervase labored on the English mission over two years before arrest and banishment in June 1606. A Roman pilgrimage followed, then, refused by the Jesuits, he took the Benedictine habit at Douai. Against his brother's wish for a safe living near Lille, he returned to England, was arrested, and refused the new oath of allegiance. Convicted merely of being a priest, he was hanged, drawn, and quartered in April 1608.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-andr:
Giovanni Andrea Cortese, known in religion as Gregorio, was a cardinal and Benedictine reformer born at Modena in 1483, who died in 1548. Trained in humanities and law, he took his doctorate at seventeen and served Cardinal Giovanni de' Medici as legal auditor. In 1507 he left the Curia for the monastery of Polirone. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his drive for monastic and church reform.

He carried the Cassinese reform through Italy and, at Lérins from 1516, founded an academy that brought Italian humanism to French youth. Elected abbot there in 1524, he later held abbacies at Modena and Perugia. Paul III made him cardinal in 1542 and Bishop of Urbino, and set him on the committee preparing the Council of Trent. His elegant Latin letters, poems, and translation of the New Testament mark him as a leading humanist writer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-golden-rose:
The Golden Rose is a precious and sacred ornament of pure gold, made by skilled artificers, which popes have blessed each year for centuries. They confer it occasionally on illustrious churches and sanctuaries, Catholic kings or queens, princes or princesses, renowned generals, governments, or cities conspicuous for Catholic spirit and loyalty. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces a gift of esteem and paternal affection.

It is blessed on Laetare Sunday, the fourth of Lent, often called Rose Sunday. Rose-colored vestments then replace penitential purple as signs of hope and joy. The golden flower shows forth Christ and his kingly majesty. Its fragrance is the sweet odor of Christ to be spread by the faithful, and its thorns and red tint tell of his Passion. Before Sixtus IV it was a simple single rose; later it grew into a branch with leaves and many roses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grasse:
François-Joseph, Count and Marquess de Grasse-Tilly, was lieutenant-general of the naval forces, born near Toulon in 1723, who died at Paris on 11 January 1788. At eleven he entered the naval service of the Knights of Malta, then joined the French navy in 1739 and was captured and held in England for two years in 1747. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the admiral whose fleet sealed Yorktown.

After service in the Seven Years War and the East Indies, he sailed from Brest in March 1781 with twenty-three ships of the line. He fought Hood off Martinique and took Tobago in June. At Cap Français he found dispatches from Washington and Rochambeau urging cooperation against the English in Virginia. He acted promptly, and his control of the sea left only one issue at Yorktown, where Cornwallis surrendered on 19 October 1781.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-duc-de-:
French duke Henri de Joyeuse, born in 1563, lived twice as a Capuchin friar and twice as a soldier and marshal, earning Voltaire's teasing title of warrior monk. Third son of Marshal Guillaume de Joyeuse, he married Catherine de la Valette, fought Huguenots in Languedoc, and on his wife's death took the Capuchin habit as Père Ange in September 1587.

Released from vows to command in Languedoc after his brother's drowning in 1592, he made peace and became marshal of France and governor of Languedoc under Henry IV. He then rejoined the Capuchins in February 1599, preached before king and court, and served as provincial of France. He died of fever at Rivoli in 1608 on his way from Rome's general chapter, where he had been made definitor-general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-marie-g:
French cardinal Henri-Marie-Gaston Boisnormand de Bonnechose, born at Paris in 1800, moved from the magistracy to Rouen's archbishopric and the Senate. Attorney-general at Besançon in 1830, he took orders at Strasbourg and taught sacred eloquence at Besançon's higher school. After a Roman trip to settle a clash over his Philosophy of Christianity, he became superior of St. Louis in 1844.

Bishop of Carcassonne in 1847, of Evreux in 1854. Archbishop of Rouen the same year, he was made cardinal in 1863 and senator by office, defending the pope's temporal power and protesting the French army's withdrawal from Rome. In 1870, old as he was, he trekked to Versailles in winter to beg King William to cut Rouen's war contribution. Under the republic he opposed anti-congregation laws while urging deference to civil authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hesse:
Hesse is both a German tribe and a district stretching along the Lahn, Eder, Fulda, Werra, and lower Main and Rhine. Today it spans Hesse-Darmstadt, a grand duchy, and Hesse-Nassau, a Prussian province, with Kassel as capital. Its people descend from the Chatti, who, alongside the Cherusci, ruled Germany before Rome arrived, and Frankish times split their land into several counties.

Christianity reached parts of the region about 350 through St. Lubentius, and St. Goar and St. Kilian preached there in later centuries. The chief missionary was St. Boniface, who baptized counts at Amöneburg, cut down Thor's sacred oak at Geismar, and founded the first Hessian bishopric at Büraberg in 741. From Fulda and Hersfeld, founded by his disciples, Christian houses spread across the land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-house-of-guis:
The House of Guise, an offshoot of Lorraine's ducal family, played a major part in France's religious troubles during the sixteenth century. Claiming descent from Charlemagne, the Guises briefly claimed the French throne. They upheld Catholic interests firmly in France and in Scotland, where Mary Stuart and her mother Marie de Lorraine were kin.

Their own violence and their partisans' often stained their religious zeal, and it masked political plans dangerous to monarchical centralization. Their thirty-five years of ties with Spain roused French patriotic suspicion. In their favour, the entry notes, Huguenots also committed violence and appealed to England, while the Calvinist nobility threatened French unity even more. The article treats those members most notable for religious history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-incense:
Sweet smoke from tree resin, burned in worship, is the subject of this entry, which moves from nature to rite. Two resin trees supplied the ancient world, one in Arabia and one in India, and their bark yielded the gum. Blenders mixed in other scents, sometimes four kinds and sometimes as many as thirteen, to thicken the smoke and deepen the scent.

Beyond the temple, incense also served daily life as a guard against heat and weariness, much as perfume does now. The entry then turns to its place in Jewish worship and in Catholic liturgy. It closes with the practical side. The vessel called the incense boat holds incense for use. The server who carries it is the thurifer. Swings of the censer mark the rank of person or thing honored.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste de la Brosse, a Jesuit missionary born in France in 1724 and dead in 1782, carried his work to Canada in 1754 after ordination the year before. He first served the Abenaki, held posts at Quebec College, and in 1765 took over the Montagnais mission at Chicoutimi, the twenty-first Jesuit to hold it.

From Tadousac at the Saguenay's mouth, his rounds reached along the Labrador coast, to Micmac country, and east to Prince Edward Island. Beyond doctrine he gave the Montagnais lessons in reading, writing, and chant, and had an alphabet, catechism, and prayer book printed at Quebec in 1767. That catechism ranks among the first books printed in Canada.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-jacques-:
Jean-Jacques Bourassé, a French archaeologist and historian born in 1813 and dead at Tours in 1872. He trained for the priesthood in Paris and taught natural science at Tours's preparatory seminary in 1835. There he began a course in archaeology that drew notice in a field then still new in France.

Bourassé counts as a true pioneer of Christian archaeology in his country. After six years teaching dogma at the grand seminary, he quit teaching to write full time. His best-known books survey Christian archaeology, the cathedrals of France, the world's finest churches, and Romanesque churches of Touraine, grounding church art in history and place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-belasyse:
John Belasyse, Baron Belasyse, was a loyal Catholic nobleman who fought for Charles I and lived to serve James II. Born about 1614, second son of the first Lord Fauconberg, he sat for Thirsk in the Short and Long Parliaments until disabled as a Royalist. He then raised six regiments at his own expense and fought at Edgehill, Newbury, and Naseby, becoming lieutenant-general in the north and Governor of York.

After the Restoration he served as Lord-Lieutenant of the East Riding and Governor of Hull, and commanded the forces at Tangier. The Test Act of 1673 forced him as a Catholic to resign his posts. Denounced in the Oates Plot as commander of a supposed popish army, he endured long imprisonment in the Tower without trial. He was restored to favor under James II as First Lord Commissioner of the Treasury in 1687, and died in 1689.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-tasse:
Joseph Tassé was a French-Canadian writer, journalist, and senator. Born at Montreal in 1848, he studied at Bourget College in Rigaud and began editing Le Canada at Ottawa at nineteen. In 1869 he took over La Minerve, Montreal's leading Conservative paper, until 1872. He entered the House of Commons for Ottawa in 1878 and the Senate in 1891.

Tassé wrote over a hundred articles for La Revue canadienne and papers for the Royal Society of Canada. His books cover Philémon Wright and the timber trade, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Ottawa Valley, and, most importantly, Les Canadiens de l'Ouest of 1878. He lectured widely in Canada and the United States, praised for a clear and warm style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-crosse:
La Crosse is a Wisconsin diocese erected in 1868 from land north and west of the Wisconsin River. After Superior split off in 1900, it covered twenty-two counties and 17,299 square miles as a suffragan of Milwaukee.

At its founding, twenty-two priests served twenty-three churches and about fifty stations, with English, German, Polish, and Italian congregations and six parish schools. Its first bishop, Michael Heiss, born in Bavaria in 1818, came to America in 1842, built Milwaukee's first parish church in 1846, and headed St. Francis Seminary. In twelve years at La Crosse he raised churches, including the cathedral, and the bishop's house, before succeeding at Milwaukee in 1880.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-grande-cha:
La Grande Chartreuse, mother-house of the Carthusian Order, stands in a high Dauphine valley at 4,268 feet, fourteen miles from Grenoble to the north. Medieval writers marvelled at the spot's bleakness, while modern eyes praise its beauty or, like Ruskin, call its cliffs commonplace.

St. Bruno built the first house in 1084, an avalanche wrecked it in 1132, and new buildings rose on the grand cloister's site. Fire struck eight times between 1320 and 1676, and Prior Innocent Le Masson then rebuilt most of it in the solid, severe style that still shapes it. The church keeps Gothic parts from about 1320. Under the 1901 Association Laws, dragoons expelled the last monks on 19 April 1903.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-morse:
A morse, also called monille, firmula or pectorale, began as a rectangular ornamented cloth piece. It joined the two front edges of a cope near the breast so the vestment would not slip from the shoulders. Fitted with hook and eye, such pieces were often richly embroidered or set with precious stones.

The name passed to metal clasps used in their place, found in miniatures and inventories as early as the eleventh century. These clasps slowly lost practical use and turned into pure ornaments. They were sewn to the cope flaps or hooked on so they could be removed and cared for separately. That care mattered when a clasp was heavy or costly. Usually round or square in gilded silver, they bore pearls, stones, enamel, niello and figures of saints, ranking among the goldsmith's finest work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orense:
Orense, a Galician diocese suffragan to Compostela, covers nearly all its civil province plus parts of Lugo and Zamora. Its capital, a city of 14,168 on the Miño famed since antiquity for hot springs, holds a see dating certainly before the fifth century.

Braga's first council in 561 created four dioceses whose bishops signed below Orense's, and Idacius names Pastor and Siagrius consecrated at Lugo in 433, one of them for Orense. Suevians turned Arian in 464 and Catholic under Chararic about 560, and the entry follows bishops through later centuries. Suevians embraced Arianism in 464 and returned to Catholicism under King Chararic about 560.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ortolano-ferr:
Giovanni Battista Benvenuti, called Ortolano Ferrarese because his father was a gardener, painted for the Ferrara school. He was born about 1490 and dead by about 1525. Little is known of his life beyond diligent study of Raphael and Bagnacavallo at Bologna in 1512 and 1513. His work is so close to Garofalo's that critics have argued endlessly over which hand painted which picture.

His master work, rich in colour and fine in drawing, shows Saints Sebastian, Roch, and Demetrius. It now hangs in the National Gallery in London. The gallery bought it in 1861, after it left the church at Bondeno in 1844. Other pictures linked to him stand in Ferrara cathedral and its smaller churches. Further works sit in galleries at Ferrara, Naples, and Berlin, with more in private hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philosophy-of:
The philosophy of common sense was the Scottish answer to Berkeley and Hume, the phase of reaction Kant matched in Germany. Common sense here means the original principles found in all normal minds, in Fénelon's phrase the notions one can neither contradict nor examine but by which one judges everything. Locke's doctrine of ideas, borrowed from Descartes, had let Berkeley dissolve the outer world into ideas and Hume dissolve the mind into a succession of states.

Between them, subject and object vanished into scepticism. Thomas Reid, dissenting from Locke, rebuilt philosophy on principles every mind shares: the senses truly report an outer world, and the self truly endures behind its states. Later sections follow Reid's successors through the Scottish school, weighing its appeal to universal judgment against the charge that it merely baptizes prejudice. The entry treats a school, not a faculty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-buse:
Pierre Busée, also called Buys, was a Jesuit theologian born at Nijmegen in 1540. Entering the Society at Cologne at twenty-two, he became master of novices there in 1567 and taught religion to the college's higher classes. His great labour was completing Canisius's large catechism by supplying the full text of every scriptural and patristic reference the author had cited, a project Canisius himself encouraged.

The first volume appeared at Cologne in 1569 as Authoritates sacrae Scripturae. The work was complete in 1570 in four volumes, and a fine Manutius edition of 1571 lacked only the last volume for unknown reasons. A revised one-volume Opus catechisticum followed in 1577. Busée left Cologne for Vienna, lectured on Scripture at the university, and taught Hebrew at the Jesuit college. He joined the commission drafting the Ratio Studiorum at Rome in 1584 and died rector of Vienna's College of Nobles in 1587.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-relation-of-g:
The relation of God to the universe is the world's essential dependence on God, in creation and in conservation. Developing the First Cause argument, the entry holds that the world depends on God first as Creator, the producer of its whole being or substance. Once produced, its continuance at every moment rests on his sustaining power. Creation means producing a being wholly out of nothing, replacing absolute nonexistence with existence.

The Creator relation, the entry argues, is the sole way the Infinite can relate to the finite. Pantheist theories fail here: they turn the varieties of being into determinations, emanations, or phases of one eternal reality, Substance in Spinoza's system. Knowledge gained through revelation, guaranteed by infinite Truth himself, closes the discussion as the most certain knowledge we can possess.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-self-defense:
A private person who faces an unjust attack may use force in reply, and this entry sets out the moral rules that govern that right. It covers attacks on life, on the body, on property, and on good name. Catholic moralists, the entry says, agree on the main principles even where they differ on finer points. Defense of life comes first. A person may use whatever force is needed, even taking the attacker's life.

Force must stay within what is needed to defeat the attack. A slight wound or a call for help, if enough, forbids killing. The attack must have actually begun, not merely been planned. A person may also give up the right out of charity, unless duty binds him to defend himself fully. The entry goes on to defense of others, of property, and of reputation, with the same measure of restraint throughout.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sister-louise:
Sister Louise, born Josephine Susanna Vanderschriek at Bergen-op-Zoom, Holland, on 14 November 1813, died at Cincinnati, Ohio, on 3 December 1886. Tenth of twelve children of an Antwerp advocate turned woolen-cloth manufacturer, she inherited from her father skill in managing affairs, firmness on principle, and unswerving fidelity to duty. From her mother she gained a gentle disposition that endeared her to all. 

Clothed in the habit on 15 October 1837 as Sister Louise, her fervor shortened her probation. She professed vows on 7 May 1839. That same year Sister Louise joined seven others as volunteers when Bishop Purcell of Cincinnati, visiting Namur, sought sisters for his diocese. Landing at New York on 19 October 1840, they reached Cincinnati and built a province that grew to nearly twelve hundred members. A novitiate opened in America in 1846, and a second at Roxbury near Boston in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ambrose:
St. Ambrose was bishop of Milan from 374 to 397, born probably in 340 at Trier, Arles, or Lyons. He died on 4 April 397, one of the most illustrious Fathers and Doctors of the Church. This long entry sets him beside Augustine, Chrysostom, and Athanasius as upholders of St. Peter's chair. It notes that his biography must be pieced together from his own writings, since the Life by his secretary Paulinus, written at Augustine's suggestion, disappoints.

Descended from an ancient Roman family that had long embraced Christianity, counting martyrs and high officials among its members. Ambrose was born while his father, also Ambrosius, served as prefect of Gaul, ruling France, Britain, and Spain. The entry follows his rise from governor to bishop and his battles with emperors and heretics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-blaise:
St. Blaise was bishop and martyr, whose name the ninth-century martyrologies of Europe list on 15 February as Blasius, bishop of Sebaste and martyr. This entry follows the evidence with care. The Greek synaxaria list him under 11 February. The oldest known recension of the so-called martyrology of St. Jerome lacks his name, and only in the later, enlarged catalogues is he mentioned.

The historical notices about him in those martyrologies and synaxaria rest on the legendary Acts. All the statements agree that Blasius was bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, and most accounts place his martyrdom in the reign of Licinius, about 316. Those reports may rest on old traditions bound up with the saint's veneration in the Church liturgy, so they should not be absolutely rejected. Perhaps it can be assumed that Blasius was a bishop and suffered martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-louis-of-t:
Louis of Toulouse, bishop who died at twenty-three, spent seven years a hostage prince learning from Franciscans. Born at Brignoles in February 1274, he was second son of Charles II of Anjou, the Lame, king of Naples, and Mary of Hungary. Mary was great-niece of Elizabeth of Hungary, and Louis was nephew of Louis IX of France. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Brignoles to 19 August 1297.

Some early sources call him firstborn only because he succeeded to his brother Charles Martel's rights after Martel died in 1295. Louis went with two brothers to Aragon in 1288 as hostage for his father, captured in a naval battle off Naples in 1284. During seven years' captivity, 1288 to 1295, at Sciurana castle and partly at Barcelona, Franciscan friars educated the three princes. Among them were Ponzius Carbonelli, Peter of Falgar, and Richard of Middleton. From that schooling grew a bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syracuse:
Syracuse in Sicily is an archdiocese whose city stands on a peninsula reaching into the Ionian Sea near the Anapus, where papyrus still grows. Its chief harbour is Sicily's largest and among the Mediterranean's finest, guarded by two islets without blocking entry, and exports now exceed imports. The cathedral rises on a temple of Minerva that once held thirty-six columns, of which twenty-two remain.

Inside, Scilla's pictures and frescoes share space with a silver statue of Lucy and a font carved from a Greek crater on seven bronze lions from the San Giovanni catacombs. Other churches hold works by Caravaggio, Minniti, and Marabitti, civic buildings show Gothic and Moorish styles, and the museum is rich in Christian inscriptions. Ancient ruins and a full archaeology bibliography round out the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tarentaise:
Tarentaise, also called Moutiers en Tarentaise, is a diocese of the Moutiers arrondissement in Savoie, suffragan of Chambéry. Legend says James the Assyrian, secretary to Honoratus of Arles, evangelized the Centrones in the fifth century. He became first bishop of Darantasia and named Marcellus his successor. The first reliable document is Leo the Great's letter of May 450, assigning Tarentaise to Vienne.

Sanctius, at Epaon in 517, is the first historically known bishop. Frankfort in 794 heard a plea against Leo's settlement. Leo III made Darantasia a metropolis over Aosta, Sion, and Maurienne while keeping Vienne's primacy. That quarrel lasted four centuries. Saracens wrecked Darantasia in the tenth century, and archbishops moved across the Isère. Moutiers grew there, and in 1186 Barbarossa made the archbishop a prince of the empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-telese:
Telese is a small town in Benevento province, southern Italy, in the valley of the Calore, famed for hot sulfur springs. Ruins of ancient Telesia, the Tedis of Oscan coins, still stand on Monte Acerro. Hannibal captured the city in 207 BC, and Scipio founded a colony there. Fallen into decay, it was rebuilt in the ninth century. Its first bishop appears in Agnellus in 487, and by the tenth century it answered to the Archbishop of Benevento.

Bishop Gian Francesco Leoni moved the episcopal residence to Cerreto Sannita in 1612. The see later joined Piedimonte d'Alife, but was re-established in 1852. Among its bishops, Alberico Giacquinto of 1540 was famed for learning and piety. Angelo Massarelli of 1567 served as secretary of Trent and wrote its acts and a diary. Vincenzo Lupoli of 1792 was a distinguished jurisconsult. The diocese holds 24 parishes, 60,600 people, and fifty priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tenebrae-hear:
The Tenebrae hearse is the triangular candlestick used in the Tenebrae service. Its name comes through French herse from Latin herpex, a harrow, the same word now used for funeral processions. The funeral hearse was first a frame over the bier, holding the pall. It bore many prickets for burning tapers, and their likeness to harrow teeth gave it the name. Later it meant any coffin receptacle, then the vehicle carrying the dead.

The Tenebrae hearse takes its name the same way, from prickets like harrow teeth. It dates at least to the seventh century, in an ordo published by Mabillon. Candle numbers varied: Amalarius speaks of twenty-four, others of thirty, twelve, nine, or seven. Today it bears fifteen candles, all unbleached wax, though some churches put a white candle at the apex. During the service candles die one by one after each psalm, leaving only the highest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-calas-cas:
A Toulouse merchant's fate became a cause célèbre of religious tolerance, and this entry tells it plainly. Jean Calas, a French Calvinist born in 1698 near Castres, had lived some forty years in Toulouse when his son Marc-Antoine was found hanged in the family warehouse on 13 October 1761. A crowd cry turned suspected suicide into alleged murder by a father bent on blocking a conversion.

Capitouls, the city's chief magistrates, seized on the charge. Calas was tried, condemned, and executed on 10 March 1762. Voltaire took up the case, exposed the flimsy evidence, and won rehabilitation for the family. The entry follows the trial, the pamphlet war, and the verdict's reversal with sober detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-dease:
Thomas Dease, Bishop of Meath, was born in Ireland in 1568 and died at Galway in 1651. From an old landed family in Cavan and Westmeath, he learned Irish well enough to write poems in it, then trained at Paris, where he became rector of the Irish Seminary. Consecrated Bishop of Meath in 1622, he returned to Ireland under the penal laws.

Dease stayed loyal to England and preached loyalty to his flock, refusing to join the Confederation of Kilkenny despite pressure from the primate. That stance won him toleration from the government but angered fellow Catholics and the papal nuncio Rinuccini, who blamed him for sowing strife between the Confederate generals Preston and O'Neill. A false report of his death in 1648 drew little regret from the nuncio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-toulouse:
Toulouse is an archdiocese covering the department of Haute-Garonne in southern France. Re-established by the Concordat of 1802, it first held Haute-Garonne and Ariege, with the archbishop styling himself also of Auch, Narbonne and Albi. Later creations cut it back, and the bull Paternae Caritatis of July 1822 fixed it almost wholly within the old dioceses of Toulouse, Rieux and Comminges.
