The city itself, chief town of the Tectosagi, resisted Rome in the Cimbric invasion, then flourished as a Roman town with famous schools. Taken by the Goths in 413, it later passed through Frankish, Visigothic and French hands. In 1295 Boniface VIII cut off Pamiers from it, and in 1319 John XXII made Toulouse a metropolitan see, with Montauban, Saint-Papoul, Rieux and Lombez as suffragans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-universe:
Universe is taken here in the astronomical sense, from our own planet out to the starry realm. The entry treats systems of the world in the widest sense, covering the structure and motions of the heavenly bodies across past, present, and future ages. Its present system forms the subject of universal cosmography, as described by Lambert, the Herschels, Laplace, Newcomb, and others. The section at hand deals only with the solar system, and in particular with the rival theories of Ptolemy and Copernicus.

Greek astronomy opens the story, with the earliest planetary schemes of the Greek schools. fifty-bab-ballads-much-sound-and-little-:
W S Gilbert subtitled his Fifty Bab Ballads 'much sound and little sense,' collecting comic verses he first printed in the magazine Fun under editor Tom Hood. flint-and-feather-collected-verse:
Flint and Feather gathers the collected verse of E Pauline Johnson, the Canadian poet of Mohawk and English descent who performed her work across Canada and England. Johnson inscribed the book, by permission, to the Duke of Connaught as Head Chief of the Six Nations. A memorial introduction recalls her deathbed wish, her London recital tours of 1906, and a gratitude her friends describe as a passion rather than a sentiment.

Inside, the poems speak in the two voices that made her famous. Some take up Indigenous legend, land, and grievance in strong narrative lines. Others give lyrics of the Canadian woods, rivers, and seasons. A producer's note warns that later printings added a misleading subtitle claiming completeness, and that claim is dropped here. What remains is the verse collection as Johnson shaped it, framed by those who knew her.
good-sense:
Baron d'Holbach's Good Sense, subtitled Freethoughts Opposed to Supernatural Ideas, is an English translation of his French Le Bon Sens. The undated translation names no translator, and a Bacon epigraph sets its theme: atheism leaves men to sense, philosophy and laws, while superstition erects an absolute monarchy in men's minds.

Contents ask what theology is, whether man is born with religious ideas, whether belief in God is necessary, and whether all religion is absurdity. Holbach argues plainly and polemically, in short chapters meant to be read and passed on. Readers interested in Enlightenment freethought will find Good Sense one of its bluntest, most readable statements.
govdocs-archive_org-nMonroeByCapellFranc:
A second copy of Frank A. Capell's 1964 booklet on the death of Marilyn Monroe sits in the archive beside the first. Capell was an anti-Communist investigator and the editor of the Herald of Freedom, and the booklet became his best-known work.

Monroe had been found dead in 1962, officially of an overdose, and Capell argued the case was stranger than the ruling allowed. His booklet worked over the evidence and pointed readers toward darker explanations. Duplicate captures are kept so a damaged page in one copy can be checked against the other; the text is an early landmark of Monroe conspiracy writing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAEuropeSecret:
Clare Pedrick reported for the Washington Post from Rome on November 13, on a disclosure that embarrassed governments across Western Europe. Operation Gladio, a clandestine network organized with the CIA, had maintained secret armies meant to resist a Soviet invasion.

The stay-behind networks had hidden weapons and agents in NATO countries for decades, and their exposure in 1990 raised hard questions about what they had actually done in peacetime. Pedrick's dispatch carried the story to American readers as the scandal broke. The article is preserved as first-day journalism on one of the Cold War's deepest secrets.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAPressSelf-Pr:

The proposal was backed by Dallas millionaire Gordon McLendon and by David Phillips, a former CIA officer who led an association of retired intelligence officers. Director Stansfield Turner was approached, and the agency's response was 'totally noncommittal.' The article survives as a curiosity of the CIA's image problem in the exposure years, when even its publicity plans made news.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrankShirleyRos:
An FBI memorandum from Savannah, dated September 30, 1964, reports a contact by Shirley Rose Frank. Frank had approached immigration authorities with a plain statement: she wanted to go to Russia because she is a Communist. The Bureau wrote her words into a memorandum.

In 1964, an American asking to leave for Russia drew official attention by reflex. Defections ran the other way in the public mind, and Oswald's own years in Russia were fresh history. The memo preserves one woman's request and the file it created, a small record of Cold War movement and suspicion.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JacksonJesse_Ja:

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JamesRosemaryWa:

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TrialDefense_Tr: George Lardner Jr. covered the Watergate cover-up trial for the Washington Post. govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:

hanshu-ban-gu-chinese:
Ban Gu, a court scholar of the Eastern Han, wrote the Hanshu, the Book of Han, in the first century CE. It tells the story of the Western Han house, from its founding to the fall of Wang Mang. The text here is the full work in its original classical Chinese, drawn from Chinese Wikisource.

Annals of the emperors come first, then tables, then treatises on rites, law, food and goods, rivers, and the heavens. Biographies of ministers, rebels, scholars, and envoys fill the rest. The Hanshu set the form that all later Chinese dynastic histories would follow. It stays the base source for two centuries of China.
heartbreak-house:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Heartbreak House between 1913 and 1916, calling it a fantasia in the Russian manner on English themes. His long preface names the target: cultured, leisured Europe before the First World War. Shaw compares his house to the country homes in Chekhov and Tolstoy. Nice people read, talk, and do nothing while disaster loads its guns outside.

Young Ellie Dunn arrives at Captain Shotover's Sussex house, invited by his daughter Hesione Hushabye. The old captain pursues concentration and invents explosives between naps. A burglar, a romantic lady, and Ellie's broken engagement stir the weekend. Talk of money, love, and war circles without resolution. Shaw lets charm and futility share every scene. Readers get his darkest drawing-room comedy, where an idle class drifts toward a reckoning it cannot imagine.
hilda-wade-a-woman-with-tenacity-of-purp:
Grant Allen's Hilda Wade, published in 1899, was his last work, and its publishers' note tells a famous story. Allen died with the final chapter only roughly sketched. His friend and neighbour Arthur Conan Doyle discussed the plan with him, absorbed what Allen intended, and wrote the ending himself. The note calls it a beautiful and pathetic act of friendship.

Hilda Wade is a nurse at St. Nathaniel's Hospital with an uncanny gift of intuition. She serves Professor Sebastian, the great physiologist who preaches the gospel of germs. Episode by episode she reads patients, poisons, and impostors at a glance. Her tenacity of purpose aims at one hidden enemy through all the cases. The narrator, a young doctor, watches her gift with awe. Doyle's borrowed pen closes a series that joined detection to medical science.
houhanshu-fan-ye-chinese:

in-freedom-s-cause: In Freedom's Cause, G. A. Henty's Wallace and Bruce tale. Scottish freedom. This book preserves that historical novel. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.

laperouse:
Ernest Scott wrote this life of the French explorer Laperouse. A monument to Laperouse overlooks Botany Bay in Sydney, Scott notes. Many visitors see it yet know little of the man.

Chapters cover Laperouse's youth, his naval career, and his love story. The great voyage of exploration fills the middle of the book. His ships reached Botany Bay, then vanished into mystery. Captain Dillon's later discovery helped solve that loss. Scott tells a sea story that ends in one of exploration's famous puzzles. Scott writes for general readers, not naval specialists. mary-louise:

melbourne-house:
Susan Warner wrote Melbourne House under the name Elizabeth Wetherell. She had won fame as the author of The Wide, Wide World. Ward Lock issued this London copy in 1907, from the 1864 book.

A verse from Proverbs heads the title page, on a child's deeds. Daisy leads the tale, and her question opens chapter one. A pony chaise, a birthday, a ham, and strawberries follow in order. Trout, a field of battle, and a wounded hand come later in the heads. Daisy grows through small trials at home and at school. Each short head marks one step in her young moral life.
miscellaneous-prose:
George Meredith's shorter prose opens with his introduction to Thackeray's The Four Georges. Meredith traces Thackeray from his birth in Calcutta in 1811. He follows him through Charterhouse school and then Cambridge. He praises Thackeray's quiet eye, his humour, and his gift for sharp, funny criticism.

The parodies, Meredith argues, judge their targets better than grave reviews do. This volume also holds A Pause in the Strife and Concession to the Celt. A memoir of Leslie Stephen follows. model-speeches-for-practise:

His earlier books include How to Speak in Public and Great Speeches and How to Make Them. The volume opens with his own introduction on the aims and purposes of speaking.

mohammed-ali-and-his-house: Luise Mühlbach wrote this historical novel about Mohammed Ali and his house in Egypt, and Chapman Coleman translated it from the German. The two share a permanent joint interest, though the narrator never chose it. Monsieur bears an indisputable personal resemblance to him.

The gentleman never speaks, though his lips move and his face shifts with expression. He wears mourning at family funerals, and some trace his line to Spanish knights of the mirror. His botany plate names continue: Shoebootia Utilis, Washtubbia Circularis, and Tigerlillia Terribilis. Each plant is drawn as if for a serious scientific work, which is the joke. Lear, the artist who taught Queen Victoria drawing, made nonsense a form of art. Children and adults still quote his limericks and copy his absurd gardens.
more-translations-from-the-chinese:

His plain, musical versions introduced Chinese poetry to English readers who knew none of the language. mother-goose-in-prose:

The Cat and the Fiddle, the Black Sheep, and Old King Cole follow. Mistress Mary, Jack Horner, and the Man in the Moon get their tales too. Baum wrote the book before The Wonderful Wizard of Oz made him famous. His expansions give the rhyme figures families, motives, and small adventures for children who ask why.
my-strangest-case:

Catalog copy says a detective is hired to hunt two men. The pair fled with treasure found in Burma's jungles. Boothby writes in a brisk, bold style of empire adventure. Dark holes, revolvers, and falls fill the picture captions. Miss Kitwater greets Mr. Fairfax in one tense scene. The case mixes crime, travel, and greed in the author's best sensational manner.
nasa-tm-19650003083-dynamic-response-of-:
David N Bowditch and Fred A Wilcox at Lewis Research Center studied how a supersonic diffuser responds when parts of it are made to oscillate. A diffuser slows fast air inside an engine inlet. Here the moving parts were the spike and the bypass, tested one at a time.

The pair measured the size and timing shift of static pressure changes inside the diffuser. Tests ran at Mach 1.8 and Mach 2.0, with a J53 engine and three cold-pipe setups of different length. The data show how inlet pressure behaves when conditions will not sit still.
nasa-tm-19670014642-computing-the-pseudo:
Christopher R. Herron, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this computing paper in November 1966. It explains how to compute the pseudo-inverse of a matrix. The pseudo-inverse stands in for an ordinary inverse when a system of equations has none. It gives engineers and scientists a standard way to handle such problems.

Herron describes an orthogonalization algorithm that produces the pseudo-inverse, then gives a complete FORTRAN program that carries the algorithm out. The opening sections define the concept through the conditions first set down by Penrose, who called it the generalized inverse. The paper keeps to real matrices for simplicity, while noting that most results also hold for complex ones. Acknowledgments credit E. R. Lancaster for supervision and theoretical help, and G. H. Wyatt for programming skill during debugging.
nasa-tm-19670026333-modification-of-the-:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this preliminary engineering report on changes to its Optical Research Facility. The catalog record says the building modifications were made for satellite tracking with lasers. Laser tracking was then a young technique that needed purpose-fitted space, stable mountings, and carefully planned building services.

The surviving contents pages detail the services side of the project. Work covers an addition to the existing building and a separate field elevated laboratory. Plumbing sections address water, sanitary, and storm systems, plus fire protection for the field laboratory. Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning are specified for both structures. Electrical sections estimate loads and lay out power distribution, lighting, utility power, and grounding. Together they show the practical building work behind an optical tracking station.
nasa-tm-19680004519-designs-of-experimen:
Arthur G. Holms, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, presented this paper at an Army design of experiments conference in Virginia in November 1967. He treats statistical designs as telescoping sequences of blocks. Each block of trials builds on the last instead of starting over.

In his sequences, the first block's results fit a simple model. Those same results are kept and combined with new blocks, fitting richer models step by step. Nothing measured is wasted. The idea grew out of optimum-seeking experiments in alloy development. NASA had used such hunts to improve engine materials for the supersonic transport.
nasa-tm-19680017367-the-salt-specificity:
L. I. Hochstein and B. P. Dalton of Ames Research Center examine a salt-dependent enzyme in this paper, presented in May 1967. The enzyme, an NADH oxidase, came from an extreme halophile, a microbe that lives in very salty settings. It works only at high solute concentrations.

Extracts of the microbe showed the enzyme accepted several salts in place of sodium chloride. Potassium, rubidium, and cesium chlorides worked with little loss of activity. Ammonium chloride worked partly, while lithium chloride failed completely. Among anions, chloride had no unique hold either. Bromide, nitrate, and iodide were essentially ineffective, while acetate, formate, citrate, and sulfate proved suitable substitutes.
nasa-tm-19690028502-development-of-space:
C. N. Irvine, of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, reports window assembly development in this July 1969 memorandum, report number 53853. The assemblies serve a space station's pressure shell. Their special feature is explosive cutting: a shaped charge can slice a clean opening through the window panel when crews need one.

Chapters cover design and fabrication before the test series begins. Tests cut twenty-centimeter holes in panels at two charge loadings, shown in photographs. Smaller fifteen-centimeter holes follow, including a vented version and a detonator standoff trial. A pressure cartridge is pictured among the hardware. Conclusions and recommendations close the development report for the prototype assemblies.
nasa-tm-19720011008-system-evaluation-fr:
J K Baumeister and E H Hopper of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this technical note in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2521. It solves a common problem in systems analysis. Engineers often know a system only by its sampled impulse response. That list of numbers is awkward for further design work. What they really need is the transfer function, a compact formula for the system's behavior.

The authors found a procedure based on rational approximation. It computes the transfer function from a limited number of response values. The system's order does not need to be known in advance. Moving the result into the other common domain is also easy. Short, incomplete response records can still yield a usable model.
nerves-and-common-sense:
Annie Payson Call gathered Nerves and Common Sense from pieces first printed in The Ladies' Home Journal. Call also wrote Power Through Repose and As a Matter of Course. She thanks editor Edward Bok for his helpful titles. This copy is a new and enlarged edition.

Chapters treat habit and nervous strain, and how women can keep from being nervous. Others ask why Mrs Smith gets on my nerves, and deal with trying family members and irritable husbands. Call sets quiet against chronic excitement, and rest against hurry. Her counsel is plain and household sized, aimed at daily calm rather than doctors' cures.
nitro-explosives-a-practical-treatise:
P. Gerald Sanford, a public analyst for Penzance and a trained chemist, wrote Nitro-Explosives as a practical treatise. This copy is the second edition, revised and enlarged. Sanford had worked as resident chemist at explosives works in Stowmarket and Hayle. He also advised the Cotton Powder Company.

His preface promises a brief but thorough account of nitrated substances. He covers their properties, their manufacture, and how to test them. The subtitle names fulminates, smokeless powders, and celluloid among the subjects. His account of nitro-glycerine and the gelatine dynamites, he claims, beats any like book in this country. Miners, blasters, and powder makers were his readers.
notes-on-the-apocalypse:
David Steele, pastor of the Reformed Presbyterian Congregation in Philadelphia, published his Notes on the Apocalypse there in 1870. Young and Ferguson printed the book. An appendix adds dissertations on some apocalyptic symbols. Steele also adds animadversions, or sharp remarks, on readings by learned expositors in Britain and America.

He submits the work under the auspices of the Reverend John Cunningham, a missionary to the Jews in London. Events of providence, Steele writes, are the signs of the times and the counterpart of prophecy. Prophecy and providence reflect light upon each other, he argues. Only the Wonderful Counsellor, he adds, can make either clear. The book reads Revelation with strict, old faith.
on-compromise:
John Morley wrote this famous essay on truth and compromise. Macmillan first printed this edition in 1886. A note dated May 1877 explains his modest aim. Morley says an essay should only open questions. It should indicate points, suggest cases, and sketch outlines.

The opening quote stresses putting truth in first place. Morley asks when compromise betrays truth in public life. He compares England's mood with that of other countries. He traces the decay of recent hopes and aspirations. The essay shaped Victorian debate about principle in politics. It still challenges readers who face hard moral choices.
p-s-correspondence-from-mosses-from-an-o:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's sketch P.'s Correspondence, from Mosses from an Old Manse, is built on a melancholy conceit. His unfortunate friend P. has lost the thread of his life. Intervals of disordered reason jumble past and present in his mind. Without stirring from his little whitewashed room, he is nevertheless a great traveler. He meets personages long invisible to any eye save his own.

Hawthorne doubts it is mere delusion; it is a sport of the imagination given morbid energy by disease. P., who always hankered after literary fame and failed to win it by reason's light, may have stumbled on it in his misty excursions beyond sanity. His letter, dated London, February 29, 1845, begins by wondering whether he is not still an inhabitant of that wearisome little chamber.
paz-la-fausse-maitresse:
Balzac's Paz, also called La Fausse Maitresse, opens in Paris in September 1835. Clementine du Rouvre, a great heiress of the faubourg Saint-Germain, marries Comte Adam Laginski, a young Polish exile. Her spendthrift father has squandered a fortune, but uncles and aunts settle theirs on her.

Adam's friend Captain Paz shares the household and serves it with hidden devotion, for he loves Clementine in secret. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the tale into English. It is a bittersweet story from the Human Comedy about loyalty, concealment, and a love that must never speak.
pen-drawing-an-illustrated-treatise: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of Pen Drawing: An Illustrated Treatise, the title page, acknowledgements, and list of illustrations, with no instruction text visible. The title page names Charles D. Maginnis, formerly instructor in illustration at the Cowles Art School and in pen drawing at the Boston Architectural Club, in a seventh edition. The illustration list credits Joseph Pennell, Bertram G. Goodhue, Herbert Railton, and Daniel Vierge among the artists whose work the treatise uses.
podcast-joerogan-3yrKVu35uSE:
Filmmaker James Fox joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2246. Fox directs documentaries on UFO cases, built from witness interviews and official records. His visits to Rogan tend to be detailed briefings rather than loose chat, and this one follows that pattern.

Fox walks through the cases and footage he has gathered, including testimony from pilots and people who claim close encounters. Rogan asks how the film work is done and which claims Fox trusts most. For listeners who follow disclosure, the episode is a compact update on the evidence Fox finds strongest and the stories still unexplained.
podcast-joerogan-GmHwG2p_esE:
Religion scholar Gary Laderman joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1565, a rare academic visit for the show. Laderman studies how Americans handle the sacred and the profane, from funerals to fame. His subject is belief in a country that claims to have outgrown it.

He and Rogan talk about death rites, the cult of celebrities, and why sacred feelings keep surfacing in secular life. Laderman brings a professor's store of odd facts, and Rogan brings the layman's blunt questions. The episode is a thoughtful tour of American religion in disguise, told through funerals, fandom, and the things people treat as holy.
podcast-joerogan-JUePtc0bJSE:
Comedian and libertarian Dave Smith returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2474. Smith hosts Part of the Problem, a sharp political comedy show. He is a frequent and favored Rogan guest.

The pair range over war, power, and media lies with ease. Smith mixes jokes with a strict antiwar case. Rogan trusts his read on the news of the day. The episode is funny and pointed in equal parts. It suits listeners who want their liberty talk served by a comic who knows both the stage and the issues. Liberty and laughs share the mic in balance.
podcast-joerogan-OR7vtVnU5SE:
Joe Rogan turns to the alien skeletons shown in Mexico and the doctors who checked them in a segment from his show. The specimens were shown to Mexico's lawmakers and split the world at once. Rogan hosts the look at the case.

Rogan works through what the doctors claimed the scans showed and what other experts said in reply. He asks why such finds so often land in a blur of hype and fraud claims. The segment is short and hot with doubt on all sides. Listeners get the core of a wild tale. The library holds the file as an archive record, without a side taken.
poems-of-purpose:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox titled this 1919 London collection Poems of Purpose, and the contents announce their errands plainly: Happiness, Seeking for Happiness, the Things that Count, Limitless, Certitude, and Compassion. Gay and Hancock published the volume in Covent Garden in the year after the Great War ended. Wilcox believed a poem should do work in a reader's life, and these pieces are tools, each built to deliver one usable thought.

Love in several states runs through the list, Love itself, Three Souls, and When Love Is Lost, beside civic pieces such as America and War Mothers. A Good Sport opens the book, and Gypsying closes it, framing duty with freedom. Taken with her other themed volumes, Purpose shows the system behind Wilcox's fame: sort the feelings of ordinary life, and give each one a short, rhymed, memorable treatment.
poise:
D. Starke wrote Poise: How to Attain It, translated by Francis Medhurst and published in the Mental Efficiency Series in 1916. Its motto states the doctrine in one line: poise is a power derived from the mastery of self. Part one argues the need, naming timidity and awkwardness as enemies that have always held capable people back. That is true never more than in the demanding life of today, where first impressions decide so much.

Part two gives the method, contrasting modesty with effrontery and prescribing physical exercises in four series, plus practical drills, toward what Starke calls the supreme achievement. The book belongs to the era's self-culture shelf, beside memory training and will-power manuals, and its premise is democratic. Poise is not breeding or luck but a trainable habit of body and nerve that any reader can practice.
popular-tales-from-the-norse:
Sir George Webbe Dasent translated and introduced this famous gathering of Norwegian folk tales, collected by Asbjörnsen and Moe and Englished for the first time here. Dasent fronts the tales with a long introductory essay on the origin and diffusion of popular tales. Arguing that stories travel across nations like seeds on the wind, and a chapter on Norse mythology to arm the reader. The tales then speak for themselves, in Dasent's hearty, fireside voice.

East o' the Sun and West o' the Moon leads the beloved titles, with Why the Sea Is Salt. The Giant Who Had No Heart in His Body, the Mastermaid, the Princess on the Glass Hill, and the boy Boots, who out-eats a troll and outwits everyone. Dasent's versions fixed these stories in English childhood. Generations learned the stumpy-tailed bear and Gudbrand on the Hillside from these pages.
power-through-repose:
Annie Payson Call wrote Power Through Repose, a new edition with additions of her influential book on relaxation. Her motto, borrowed from François Delsarte, states the creed: personality binds, universality expands. A second epigraph from W. R. Alger pictures the body perfectly adjusted, perfectly supplied with force, and working with the greatest economy, fitted to be a perfect instrument of impression, experience, and expression.

Her first chapter, the Guidance of the Body, complains that shelves groan with advice on food, air, and clothing while nobody teaches the better use of the machine itself. Strain, she argues, can be studiously abandoned through training as regular as any muscle work, climbing back step by step from perverted habits to an orderly life. Call's book founded a school of American relaxation teaching; nervous readers of the 1890s treated it as medicine.
proposals-for-building-in-every-county-a:
An unnamed writer laid a plan before Parliament in a pamphlet printed in London in 1677, urging that every county build a working almshouse or hospital. The aim was twofold: to employ the poor and to grow a home trade in linen cloth.

The plan promises work and keep for poor people and children from age five or six, an end to begging, and relief for parishes crushed by poor rates. It also promises to keep at home the large sums then spent abroad on linen. Readers get an early scheme of workhouse reform.
punky-dunk-and-the-mouse:
Punky Dunk and the Mouse is a picture book in rhyme for small children, issued by P. F. Volland and Company of Chicago under a 1912 copyright. Like its companions in the series, it names no author, and its title page leaves a blank line for the name of the child it was made for.

The sly kitten spends a morning in the cellar hunting a fat little mouse. He sits by the mouse's hole near the coal, beside a trap baited with cheese, and pretends to nap while he watches for the gleam of two bright eyes. Soon the mouse creeps out and runs about, and Punky smiles to himself.
raabe-die-chronik-der-sperlingsgasse:
An old man looks back over the life of one Berlin street in Raabe's first novel, Die Chronik der Sperlingsgasse, given here in German. The Chronicle of Sparrow Lane gathers neighbors, loves, and losses into a single remembered neighborhood. Raabe published the book at twenty-five, and it announced a major talent.

Warm, nostalgic, and beautifully observed, the novel made readers call its author the German Dickens, a name that stuck. Each household on the lane opens like a small world with its own weather. Joy and grief share doorsteps in his telling. The book remains the friendliest doorway into Raabe's long career. Its lane still feels inhabited, door by door.
red-pepper-s-patients-with-an-account-of:
Grace S. Richmond returned to her doctor hero in this 1918 book from Doubleday, Page, printed at Garden City, New York. Its full title singles out one case: Anne Linton's, in particular. A front picture shows Red Pepper Burns, M.D., at work among those he treats.

Chapters open with an intelligent prescription and a place called Little Hungary, then turn to Anne Linton's temperature. Two red heads, heavy local mails, white lilacs, and expert diagnosis fill the middle list. One chapter is named The Surgical Firing Line, and another The Truth About Susquehanna. The cases mix town practice with strain, love, and risk.
sanguozhi-chen-shou-chinese:
Chen Shou, an official of the Jin court, wrote the Sanguozhi, the Records of the Three Kingdoms, around 289 CE. After the Han fell, China split into Wei, Shu, and Wu, and Chen Shou gave each state its own book. The text here is the full work in classical Chinese, from Chinese Wikisource.

The records are built from biographies: founders, generals, ministers, and queens, each life packed with deeds and judgments. Chen Shou wrote close to the events, from court files and fresh memory. His book is the base source for the Three Kingdoms age. The famous novel of that age grew from these dry, sharp lives.
scotus-ordinatio-opus-oxoniense:
Scotus's Ordinatio, long known as the Oxford Work, appears here in the 1891 Vives printing of his collected works. The Ordinatio is his great commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, the set text of medieval theology. Scotus lectured on the Sentences at Oxford, and the work grew into his summa, left unfinished at his death in 1308.

Across its books, the commentary treats God, creation, the Incarnation, and the sacraments with unmatched subtlety. Scotus defends the freedom of the will and the special privilege of Mary, doctrines that marked his school for centuries. The text is dense because the questions were hard and the standards exact. The Vives edition, reprinting Wadding's older collection, was the standard nineteenth-century way to read the Subtle Doctor's whole theology in one vast work.
seven-maids-of-far-cathay-being-english-:
Bing Ding compiled these English notes from a Chinese class book, with pictures by Ai Lang. Seven girls in the graduating class of the Woman's Anglo-Chinese College at Neuchang wrote the notes as a game across their last six months. A stenographer took the pieces down as the girls read them aloud.

College leaders arranged the notes and printed them just as first produced, with no revision. Sections bear plain role names: Biographer, Correspondent, Diarist, Essayist, Folklorist, and Genius. Western readers meet Chinese students' fresh English voices, full of humor and pride in their college life.
sex-and-common-sense:
A. Maude Royden, assistant preacher at the City Temple in London from 1918 to 1920, wrote this plain talk on relations between the sexes. Royden opens by calling the sex problem a noble one, fit for open thought rather than whispers and jokes. She insists that most readers care about normal life, not vice.

Royden argues that the sex instinct ranks among the great powers of human nature, and that its misuse brings shame and pain. She asks how plain men and women can live on a higher, finer pattern. Her aim is growth: rightly, gladly, and humanely ordered love.
shiji-sima-qian-chinese:
Sima Qian, the grand historian of the Han court, finished the Shiji, the Records of the Grand Historian, around 91 BCE. His father began the work, and Sima Qian gave it its final shape after shame and prison. The text here is the complete work in classical Chinese, from Chinese Wikisource.

One hundred thirty chapters mix basic annals, tables, treatises on rites and the heavens, the tales of great houses, and lives of single men. The reach runs from the Yellow Emperor to the reigning Han house. The Shiji founded the way China writes its past. Its biographies still set the model for Chinese prose.
sketches-from-memory-from-mosses-from-an:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote these sketches from memory for his Mosses from an Old Manse. The Notch of the White Mountains opens the set. In mid-September the party rides up the Saco valley from Bartlett, between mountain walls, along a road as level at times as a church aisle.

Height rises on height until clouds hang below the peaks. Red slide paths scar the slopes where earth, stones, and trees once thundered down. Settlers once feared northern Indians sweeping through these defiles, Hawthorne recalls. His prose turns a stage ride into awe at old, bright, perilous hills.
songs-and-other-verse:
Songs and Other Verse forms Volume IX of the Works of Eugene Field. The volume holds his writings in prose and verse. Its opening pages print a comic letter. Field signs it with a Latin-styled name, Eugenio Agro. He writes to his brother with mock pomp. He invites a bishop and his staff to a reading. Field will read his things before a senior class. The class sits at the Chicago University. Robes and a march in at eight are part of the joke.

A note then tells of a lady's trip Southwest. She won two choice gifts there for Field. For his library she got an odd Indian blanket. It shows in sketches of his loved workshop. For Field himself she got a necktie. A diamond-back rattlesnake gave its skin for it.
songs-before-sunrise: Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote Songs Before Sunrise, first published by Ellis in 1871. The 1917 William Heinemann issue at London lists many later printings by Chatto through 1915, a Florence Press edition of 1909, and a place in the Collected Poems. Swinburne gives the book to Joseph Mazzini. His dedication tells Mazzini to take the poems, since he bade them bear his name, as fruit of the seed of his sowing, be it blossom, berry, or weed.
sonnets-and-verse:
H. Belloc gives Sonnets and Verse to John Swinnerton Phillimore. A dedication poem opens the gift. It looks back to the days of boyhood. When you and I were little tiny boys, he writes. We took a bold delight in foolish toys. Painted and misshapen, mothers brought them at night. Duckworth and Co. printed the London book. Turnbull and Spears of Edinburgh made it.

Belloc asks his friend to take the flawed toys. Phillimore keeps the child's keener part, he says. In his heart the toys may gain a perfect form. The gift rests on the content a known love brings. Set at the head of sonnets and verse, the poem frames the set. Youth's toys go to an old friend. Love, the poem hopes, will mend their shape.
sonnets-from-the-portuguese: Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote Sonnets from the Portuguese, printed by the Caradoc Press at Bedford Park, Chiswick, London, in MDCCCCVI, that is, 1906. The opening pages give an index of first lines in place of the poems' text. It begins: I thought once how Theocritus had sung; But only three in all God's universe; Unlike are we, unlike, O princely Heart; and Thou hast thy calling to some palace-floor. Go from me and If thou must love me stand in the list.
stray-pearls-memoirs-of-margaret-de-riba:
Stray Pearls: Memoirs of Margaret de Ribaumont, Viscountess of Bellaise, by Charlotte M. Yonge, dated 1883 in this printing, tells a French family's story across the wars of the Fronde. Its chapter heads move between the English and French courts of the seventeenth century.

The contents begin at Whitehall before the cobwebs, pass through a little mutual aversion, Celadon and Chloe, and the Salon Bleu, then reach life in garrison and a victory dearly bought. Widow and wife, Marguerite to the rescue, the firebrand of the Bocage, the two queens, cavaliers in exile, and the barricades follow. Yonge mixes court intrigue with family duty and faith.
studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-volume-:
Volume III of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, dated 1927, holds Analysis of the Sexual Impulse, Love and Pain, and The Sexual Impulse in Women. A preface to the second edition reports the volume fully revised and enlarged, with new case histories added in an appendix.

Ellis says the main doctrines of ten years before still stand. Yet new work on hormones had reshaped knowledge in the field. Those hormones are the internal secretions of the ductless glands. They bear on how the sexual instinct is produced in the body. His own account ties the impulse to a physical process of building and release, while claiming it can stand apart from unsettled questions of ultimate origin.
sunrise:
William Black, author of Shandon Bells and Strange Adventures of a Phaeton, published the novel Sunrise at New York through John B. Alden in 1883. Its chapter titles promise travel and intrigue: a first interview, pleadings, a house in Curzon Street, pioneers, and a night in Venice.

Later chapters bring a Russian episode, a man named Calabressa, an evening at the Culturverein, a performance of Fidelio, and a father and daughter at odds. Black sets private feeling against secret societies and foreign politics, moving his people from London drawing rooms to Italy and beyond. The chapter heads, from Jacta Est Alea, the die is cast, onward, mark a story of vows, evasions, and a talisman.
susan-lenox-her-fall-and-rise:
David Graham Phillips's Susan Lenox: Her Fall and Rise appears here in Volume I of the D. Appleton edition of 1917, printed at New York and London with a portrait of the author. A tribute at the front mourns Phillips himself, written by a friend who still looks for his tall, boyish figure on Fifth Avenue.

The tribute calls Phillips the most honest man its writer ever knew. His clear blue eyes scorned untruth. His knightly mind hoisted the burdens of the world. It set them onto young shoulders, his own. The novel behind that praise follows its title's hard arc: a country girl's fall into the city's underworld and her long climb back, told with Phillips's usual anger at sham and corruption.
the-after-house:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote The After House. It is a mystery novel in twenty-five chapters, told in the first person. Chapter heads promise a painted ship and a terrible night. A found axe, prisoners, and mutiny talk come next. Tales from the stewardess, the first mate, and Oleson fill the late heads.

Chapter one, I Plan a Voyage, tells how the narrator was funded. A bequest from an elder brother paid his way. It saw him through a small Ohio college. It paid for four years at a medical school in the East. He says he hardly knows why he chose medicine. A bent for the surgeon's bold trade may explain it. A family line of doctors may explain it too. Readers board a yacht where wealth, drink, and an axe murder trap a small crew at sea.
the-angel-in-the-house:
Coventry Patmore's long poem on wedded love appears here in Cassell's National Library, printed at London in 1891. Patmore inscribes the poem to the memory of her by whom and for whom, he says, he became a poet. An introduction tells how the work first came out in two parts, in 1854 and 1856.

The editor notes that Patmore later reworked the poem with great care. It has since won, the note claims, a lasting place among the home books of the English people. Cheap wide spread, Patmore felt, would not hurt a finer library edition. The best use of writing, he held, is the spread of verse given to the sacred love of home.
the-ballad-of-the-white-horse:
G. K. Chesterton warns readers in a prefatory note that his ballad does not claim to be history. Alfred is a real king, he argues, but the legends about him are the most important thing. Chesterton deals with Alfred as a popular legend still alive in England.

Three tales show his method. One links Alfred's final victory to the Vale of the White Horse in Berkshire. Others tell of Alfred playing the harp in the Danish camp, and of Alfred with a woman and her cakes. Chesterton picks each tale because people told it, not because records prove it. The poem follows old ballad makers, who wrote from hearsay and tradition.
the-book-of-nonsense:
Edward Lear made the Book of Nonsense, a set of short comic verses with his own drawings. He gave the book to the great-grandchildren, grand-nephews, and grand-nieces of Edward, 13th Earl of Derby. Most of the verses and art were first made for their parents. A short verse at the front tells of an Old Derry down Derry who made a book to make small folk shake with glee.

Each verse takes one odd soul and spins a small joke in five lines. An old man finds that two owls, a hen, four larks, and a wren have built nests in his beard. A young lady of Ryde buys clogs and small spotty dogs and walks about Ryde. An old man with a long nose snaps that those who think it too long are wrong.
the-butterfly-house:
Mary E. Wilkins Freeman wrote The Butterfly House, put out in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1912, with illustrations by Paul Julien Meylan. Freeman had also written A Humble Romance and A New England Nun. Chapter I is spent on its setting: Fairbridge, a little New Jersey village, or rather city. It had won municipal government some years before, over the protest of far-seeing citizens.

Fairbridge, the tale says, was a misnomer. A first-time visitor, driven round its rural streets, would ask: why Fairbridge? Bridges there were none, save those the trains thundered over to and from New York. Nor could an unbiased eye call the place fair. Worse than the name was the spirit: Fairbridge was tragically petty, since it saw itself great, and narrowness there did not reign but tyrannised.
the-cab-of-the-sleeping-horse: John Reed Scott wrote The Cab of the Sleeping Horse, put out in New York by the A. L. Burt Company in 1916, by arrangement with G. P. Putnam's Sons. William van Dresser drew the front plate. Scott had also written The Woman in Question and The Man in Evening Clothes. The chapters start with The Photograph, The Voice on the Wire, and Visitors. Surprises, The Story, Decoyed, and Skirmishing lead to Half a Lie. Carpenter, The Marquis, and The Slip of Paper close the heads shown.
the-canadian-photoplay-title-of-the-land:
The Canadian is the photoplay title of The Land of Promise, a novelization by D. Torbett of W. Somerset Maugham's play, made into a Paramount Picture starring Thomas Meighan. Grosset and Dunlap published it, under a copyright of 1914 held by Edward J. Clode, and a plate caption promises the moment when love for her husband is finally born in Nora.

Chapter I opens on Nora waking to a sense of well-being, her youth reasserting itself after whatever strain came before. The book is a film tie-in of its era: a stage play turned stage story turned screen vehicle, carrying its heroine's slow change of heart as the advertised heart of the plot.
the-christmas-banquet-from-mosses-from-a:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this tale, drawn from his unpublished Allegories of the Heart and framed by talk in a summer house. Roderick unfolds a few sheets of manuscript for Rosina and the sculptor. His former sad experience, he says, has given him insight into the gloomy mysteries of the human heart.

Roderick compares that wandering to being lost in a dark cavern with a torch fast dying. Yet one figure still puzzles him past solving. The man looks like a man, perhaps a better specimen than most, and seems wise, refined, and outwardly moral. The sculptor could carve his shape in marble, and some future science might lend him a fine mockery of mind. Still, Roderick argues, the last touch of a divine Creator is lacking. What the spirit demands from another spirit, this figure cannot give.
the-circular-staircase:
Mary Roberts Rinehart built this mystery around a country house and its staircase, told by the woman who rented the house. The contents run to thirty-four chapters, with titles that name a link cuff-button, a sprained ankle, a hole in the wall, and a ladder out of place. Names recur through the list: Halsey, Gertrude, Louise, and Thomas.

Chapter I opens the narrator's own account in her voice. She calls it the story of how a middle-aged spinster lost her mind, deserted her city home, and took a furnished house for the summer. That dry self-mockery sets the tone for the puzzles that follow. A bank, a disappearance, a tramp with toothache, and Anne Watson's story all enter the contents. Rinehart mixes household comedy with steady dread, and the house itself, its corridors, stairs, and fireplaces, becomes the center of the case.
the-complete-book-of-cheese: Bob Brown wrote this cheese book, published in New York by the Gramercy Publishing Company in 1955, with illustrations by Eric Blegvad. Only the title page and a list of Brown's other food books are present here. The list names The Wine Cook Book and The South American Cook Book. It names many more besides, plus books written with the Browns as co-authors.Front matter alone is a thin basis, and it is all there is.
the-country-house: John Galsworthy's The Country House, dated 1907, is shown here only through its contents. Part I lists ten numbered chapters and Part II begins a fresh run of numbered chapters, reaching at least VII in what is present. No chapter titles are given, and the novel's own pages do not appear here.
the-dark-house:
I. A. R. Wylie, author of The Daughter of Brahma and The Shining Heights, published The Dark House in 1922. Part I opens on a large cigar and a small boy: at the moment Robert Stonehouse leans out of an upstairs bedroom window for fresh air, he turns eight years old.

Robert recalls a fifth birthday when he danced on his mother's bed shouting his age. He received a toy fort garrisoned with Highland soldiers from his father, and ruled a party of children he disliked. Soon after, his mother disappeared; they said she was dead. He picked flowers from other graves at Kensal Green to send her, never missed her, and hated Christine, who tried to take her place. Later his mother returned by a secret path as a creature of dreams, tall and beautiful, whom he refuses to believe is dead.
the-divine-comedy-volume-3-paradise:
Paradise closes Charles Eliot Norton's three-volume prose Divine Comedy. Its contents list traces the climb sphere by sphere. The Moon holds broken vows. Mercury holds Justinian's tale of the Roman eagle. Venus holds famed lovers. The Sun holds Thomas Aquinas and the wise. Each canto is summed up in a few plain lines before the text.

Higher spheres hold warriors of the faith, just rulers, and monks at prayer. Dante is quizzed on faith, hope, and love. The summaries give first-time readers a firm map of the poem's most abstract and bright realm.
the-dog-s-book-of-verse: J. Earl Clauson gathered The Dog's Book of Verse, printed in Boston with a 1916 copyright. A short verse at the front gives a dog's boast: never barking out of season, never biting without cause. The book is set in memory of Jack, an Airedale. Its first part is named Puppyhood, and a contents list sorts poems by theme. Only the front matter and that list are present here.
the-elene-of-cynewulf-translated-into-en:
Lucius Hudson Holt rendered The Elene of Cynewulf into English prose for Yale Studies in English, printed by Henry Holt in 1904. The poem opens with a count of years: two hundred and thirty-three winters since Christ's birth, in the sixth year of Constantine's reign over the Romans. Constantine stands as a shield to his folk, raised up by God with might.

Elene, the emperor's mother, sails to find the true cross. Cynewulf, an Anglo-Saxon poet, signed this tale of vision, battle, and a buried cross brought to light. Holt's prose keeps the old verse's grave pace.
the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse:
Vicente Blasco Ibanez wrote The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse as a novel of the Great War, turned into English by Charlotte Brewster Jordan. Three parts trace the Desnoyers family from Argentina to France.

The contents name Madariaga, the centaur, a rich ranch lord, and his kin split between France and Germany. Part two turns to the retreat, the invasion, and the banner of the Red Cross. Part three ends after the Marne, among burial fields. Ibanez sets one family's split loves against the four riders of war, pestilence, famine, and death let loose on Europe.
the-ghost-of-guir-house:
Charles Willing Beale wrote The Ghost of Guir House as a tale of mystery, printed in 1897. A mis-sent letter opens the tale on a dark night in New York.

Mr. Henley comes home to his small house in Twentieth Street to find a letter that has chased its man through crossed-out addresses. One note on it reads: Dead. Try Paul. The letter, dated from Guir House in September 1893, tells its reader he is the man long sought, though the two have never met. Beale draws Henley by slow steps into a haunted house, a lost will, and a love bound up with both.
the-girl-aviators-sky-cruise: Margaret Burnham wrote The Girl Aviators' Sky Cruise. Hurst and Company printed it in New York in 1911. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of twenty-four chapters. The heads promise flight and plot. They name a new venture at Sandy Beach, a naval visitor, and a storm aloft. They name Peggy as heroine, lost drawings, and the flight of the Silver Cobweb. They also name an aerial post office, a marked bill, and a final gathering of the man-birds.
the-golden-house:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote The Golden House. Chapter I opens near midnight in a famous city studio. A picked crowd of a hundred guests has come. They will see a veil lifted from an Oriental and ancient art. The late hour gives the night a feel of moral risk. The risk feels bravely run.

Warner lists the guests with sly care. Scholars of Greek beauty came from Boston. Fair women came from Washington. Stars of official and diplomatic life came too. Most guests are from the city itself. The scene mocks a rich set. That set treats a hint of scandal as high culture. It sets the tone for a novel of wealth and show, where a golden house hides thin morals.
the-green-mouse: Robert W. Chambers wrote The Green Mouse. Edmund Frederick made the pictures in color. The book is dated 1910. It is dedicated to the author's friend John Corbin. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the dedication verses, and the start of a contents list. The first heads are An Idyl of the Idle and The Idler. The third head is The Green Mouse. No chapter text is present.
the-grey-brethren-and-other-fragments-in: Michael Fairless wrote The Grey Brethren and Other Fragments in Prose and Verse. Duckworth and Company published the book in London in 1911. This is the third impression. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a prefatory note. The note asks indulgence for the little book. Its true unity lies deeper, the note says. It lies in the personal gift, the communication of heart to heart. Most of its pieces appeared before, in The Pilot.
the-hall-of-fantasy-from-mosses-from-an-:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote The Hall of Fantasy, a sketch taken from Mosses from an Old Manse. The narrator describes a vast hall with a white marble floor, a high dome, and long rows of pillars in mixed styles. Light falls through stained and pictured glass, so the room feels like a dream that a stamp of the foot might break.

A friend inside explains the place in plain terms. The hall holds for the world of fancy the same place that an exchange holds for trade. All who have business with dreams may meet there and talk it over. Upper rooms are said to reach toward the moon, while cells below lead down to darker regions.
the-happy-days-of-the-empress-marie-loui: Imbert de Saint-Amand wrote The Happy Days of the Empress Marie Louise. Thomas Sergeant Perry translated the book. The contents trace a life in order. Early chapters cover her first years and the year 1809. Later chapters cover the wedding talks and the betrothal. The story goes on to the wedding at Vienna. It ends with the entrance into Paris and the religious ceremony. Front matter is all that is present here. The chapters themselves do not appear.
the-hero-of-hill-house: Mabel Hale wrote The Hero of Hill House. The contents list chapters about a boy named Austin. Early titles include Home and Mother and The Stricken Home. Later titles include Austin and His Father. The list goes on to The Runaway and Wayside Friends. Still later titles include The Revival and The Battle of Two Wills. The last title shown is Like the Troubled Sea. What is present here stops with the front matter. The story itself does not appear.
the-inner-house:
Walter Besant wrote this novel. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in 1888. His other books include All Sorts and Conditions of Men. The prologue is set at the Royal Institution. A visiting professor will announce a great discovery there. The theatre is crammed for his lecture. The director rushes to greet him. The physicist confides his timeline. Conviction came five years earlier. Proof came only in the last six months.

For half a year, rumors had flown from his laboratory. The place was Ganzweltweisst am Rhein. Guesses filled the papers of two continents. Some said he had learned to make food from chemicals. Others said he could send matter through space at once. Others feared a weapon that could shatter armies. Besant frames his tale with that comedy of guessing. The discovery itself would change how men live together.
the-intelligence-office-from-mosses-from:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's sketch opens in a metropolitan office. A grave figure sits at a desk in the corner. Mysterious spectacles rest on his nose. A pen sits behind his ear. He pores over a folio of ledger size. The walls carry advertisements of every kind. Articles lost, wanted, or for sale cover them. He looks like the spirit of a record. His own great volume seems made visible in him.

Customers stream in from the busy street. A mechanic seeks a cheap tenement. An Irish girl wanders from kitchen to kitchen. Her heart still hangs in her native cottage smoke. A faded beauty asks for her lost bloom. Peter Schlemihl asks for his lost shadow. An author seeks his vanished reputation. Then a misfit enters, hat awry and eyes astray. He announces that this must be the Central Intelligence Office.
the-judgment-house: Gilbert Parker wrote this South Africa novel, its contents running to thirty-nine chapters. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story does not appear. The headings mix the personal and the political. The jasmine flower and a daughter of Tyre open them. The partners meet, and a woman tells her story. The power-house and three years later follow. An arrow finds a breast midway. Wales appears, where Jigger plays his part. The Baas comes, a fiery furnace burns, and a battle cry closes the list.
the-lay-of-marie-and-vignettes-in-verse:
Matilda Betham published her poem The Lay of Marie in 1816, and a later Garland reprint joins it with her 1818 Vignettes in Verse. Donald H. Reiman supplies an introduction for that reprint. The poem opens with a long dedication in verse to Lady Bedingfeld.

Betham asks who else should receive a theme of minstrel lore drawn from earlier times. She praises her friend love of heroes and fair dames kept alive by romance and song. The dedication blends friendship, admiration, and esteem in formal couplets before the lay itself begins on medieval material.
the-leavenworth-case: Anna Katharine Green subtitled her detective novel a lawyer story. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. Book one chapters cover a great case and a coroner inquest. Facts and deductions, a clue, expert testimony, and Mary Leavenworth follow in the list. Book two, headed Henry Clavering, begins in the list as well. The investigation of the Leavenworth murder, and detective Gryce work in later chapters, does not appear in this record beyond those titles.
the-lerouge-case: Emile Gaboriau wrote his French detective novel, first published in 1863 according to the record heading. Only the title page and a bare contents list of nineteen numbered chapters are present here, with no chapter titles and no story text at all. The murder inquiry that made Gaboriau famous, and his detective Lecoq, cannot be seen in this record beyond the book name and its author.
the-life-and-perambulations-of-a-mouse:
Dorothy Kilner wrote her children tale in 1783 and 1784, and an introduction sets the storytelling scene. A severe winter snow confines a large party at Meadow Hall, where young folk and elders share the shelter. Mornings go to reading, and the rest of the day to dancing, singing, and games.

When known stories run out, a sprightly girl proposes that each person tell the history of their own life. A mouse narrator fits that game in the tale proper. Kilner uses an animal voice to teach children manners, kindness, and care in daily conduct.
the-lighthouse: R. M. Ballantyne, author of The Coral Island, wrote his tale of the Bell Rock lighthouse for young readers. Only the title page and a detailed contents list are present here. Twenty-nine chapters cover a press gang, a burglary, and storms on the Pharos. Life in the beacon, smugglers dosed with gin, and the lighthouse completed close the plan. A hero named Ruby runs through the chapter titles from trouble to rise in life. The tale itself is missing from this record.
the-little-lady-of-the-big-house:
Jack London's The Little Lady of the Big House opens with rancher Dick Forrest waking in the dark on his sleeping-porch. Forrest knows himself at once, master of broad acres, and listens with pleasure to the distant bawl of King Polo, his champion Short Horn bull. He plans new triumphs for the bull on the Eastern livestock circuits, meaning to prove that a California-born animal can beat corn-fed Iowa stock and imported bulls alike.

Rows of electric buttons beside his bed light the porch, a clock, a barometer, and thermometers. London builds the scene around wealth, machinery, and exact control of a great ranch. Readers meet a confident, rich cattleman at the height of his powers before the little lady of the title enters his ordered world.
the-lost-house:
Richard Harding Davis opens The Lost House on a dull day at the American chancellery in London. The ambassador is in Scotland unveiling a bust of Bobby Burns, the First Secretary watches a sham battle at Aldershot, and the attachés are at a football match and a pheasant shoot. The Second Secretary, alone, has just confided a state secret to his friend Austin Ford, the London correspondent of the New York Republic. Ford promises to cable it disguised as news from a Hungarian diplomat en route to Patagonia.

He really came, though, to ask about an international polo match. The Secretary begins a lecture: polo is a proposition of ponies, since men can be trained but ponies must be born. A page then interrupts with a visitor carrying an important note for the ambassador.
the-love-chase: James Sheridan Knowles wrote The Love-Chase, issued by Cassell and Company in London in 1887. Only the title page, the cast list, and the first stage direction are present here, so the comedy itself does not appear. The cast list preserves the original Haymarket performance of 1837, naming the actors: Mr. Strickland as Sir William Fondlove, Mr. Elton as Waller, who loves Lydia, Mr. Webster as the sportsman Wildrake, and Mrs. Glover as Widow Green. The scene is London, and act one opens in the lobby of an inn.
the-man-who-could-not-lose:
Richard Harding Davis's The Man Who Could Not Lose opens on a marriage made in haste that refused to repent at leisure. Champ Carter and his wife are so in love that they count the marriage their greatest asset; their friends count it the only thing against either of them. Champ, raised rich, was left by his father's death with no money and a few debts of honor. He has been paying them off ever since Yale by living on his pen, writing slowly for slow editors. Dolly Ingram's trouble is her mother, a leader of terrifying exclusiveness.

Widowed with millions to dispose of as she pleased, Mrs. Ingram keeps one ambition unfulfilled: to marry Dolly to an English duke. She has a shopworn duke, a bankrupt duke, and a young one in training.
the-maternal-management-of-children-in-h:
Thomas Bull, a London physician and lecturer on midwifery and the diseases of women and children, published The Maternal Management of Children, in Health and Disease in 1840. His preface addresses the young and inexperienced mother directly. Bull says such mothers almost never possess the knowledge his experience shows they need. Ignorance, he warns, has injured many infants' constitutions and cost some their lives.

The opening chapters cover the general management of the child in health. Bull teaches that prevention of disease is the mother's province, not its cure. He warns her never to tamper with medicine once illness has actually begun. A later chapter shows parents how to detect the first symptoms of disease early. Readers get a Victorian doctor's plain rules for nurseries, written before modern pediatrics existed.
the-mistress-of-the-manse:
J. G. Holland's The Mistress of the Manse, published in New York by Scribner, Armstrong and Co. in 1874, is a story told in verse. A short contents page names a prelude and three movements: Love's Experiments, Love's Philosophies, and Love's Consummations. The poem's shape is therefore a courtship and marriage followed through stages.

Love's Experiments opens as a crowd leaves a gate and a dusty coach draws up. The pastor and his bride step out and pass through a waiting door that closes on the watching street. Philip can only cry his wife's name, and Mildred answers that she is home, the old life closed and the new before them. Inside, the maid Dinah announces the mistress of the house.
the-new-adam-and-eve-from-mosses-from-an:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's tale The New Adam and Eve imagines the human race swept away while everything people made remains standing. The Day of Doom, following Father Miller's reading of prophecy, empties cities, fields, and islands of every living thing. Houses, tools, and all the footprints of human work stay untouched. A new Adam and a new Eve, created grown in mind and heart but knowing nothing of their predecessors, inherit the deserted earth.

Hawthorne proposes, half sportive and half thoughtful, to follow the pair through their first day. Such innocents, he argues, would at once tell art from nature, finding wisdom and simplicity in the one and elaborate puzzles in the other. Dawn comes with no human eye to see the east blush.
the-odyssey-rendered-into-english-prose-: Homer's Odyssey is rendered into English prose for readers who cannot read the original Greek. Only the front matter is present here, together with the start of a preface, so the epic itself does not appear. A dedication in Italian thanks Professor Biagio Ingroia as a precious ally. The contents list prefaces to two editions, all twenty-four books, and footnotes. The preface begins by saying the translation was meant to supplement another work, though the sentence breaks off.
the-old-manor-house:
Charlotte Smith published the novel The Old Manor House in 1793, in two volumes of numbered chapters. The pages present here give a life of the author before the contents. Charlotte Turner Smith was born in London in 1749, married at fifteen to pay her father's gambling debts, and endured a violent, wasteful husband.

Her life shaped her writing. She wrote Elegiac Sonnets in 1784 while living with her husband in a debtors' prison, and the book's success freed them. Her first novel, Emmeline, came in 1788, followed by nine more. A family inheritance stayed tied up in lawsuits for forty years, and she died in 1806 after years of debt and illness.
the-old-manse-from-mosses-from-an-old-ma:
Nathaniel Hawthorne introduces readers to his home in The Old Manse, the opening piece of Mosses from an Old Manse. He describes a gray old parsonage at the end of an avenue of black-ash trees, its gate long fallen from its hinges. A year has passed since the funeral of the aged clergyman who last lived there.

Hawthorne notes that no layman had lived in the house before him. A priest built it, priests followed, and the last minister alone wrote nearly three thousand sermons there. The new tenant, ashamed of his idle tales, hopes wisdom will fall on him with the leaves of the avenue.
the-old-stone-house:
Anne March, the pen name of Constance Fenimore Woolson, wrote The Old Stone House. The contents list eleven chapters, from The Five Cousins to a conclusion. Chapter One opens on Aunt Faith's birthday, the first of June, as she sits alone on the piazza looking back over more than fifty years.

Aunt Faith lost her husband while still a bride, then lost her brothers and sisters one by one. She became sole guardian of their five orphan children: Hugh and Sibyl Warrington, Tom and Grace Morris, and wild little Bessie Darrell from the southern hill country. For ten years she has watched over the band, and the novel follows life in her old stone house.
the-purchase-price-or-the-cause-of-compr: Emerson Hough, already known for The Mississippi Bubble and 54-40 or Fight, published his novel in 1910 with illustrations by M. Leone Bracker and Edmund Frederick, dedicating it to Senator Albert J. Beveridge. Twenty-three chapters move from a lady in company and a gateway scene through Tallwoods, an invasion, and an argument toward a payment and a Washington close. Only the title pages, dedication, and full chapter list are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear.
the-purse:
Honore de Balzac's short tale appears here in Clara Bell's English translation, dedicated to Sofka with a note on the family likeness medieval artists gave to paired figures in adoration. The story opens at twilight, an hour Balzac treats as made for artists and dreaming.

In that softened light a young painter stands back from his work and judges it with fresh eyes, as illusion loosens the grip of daily life. Balzac lingers on how half-light changes pictures, flesh, and fabric before any plot begins. Readers who enjoy his Parisian scenes will find atmosphere and artistic ambition carrying the opening.
the-rainbow-and-the-rose: E. Nesbit's poems of 1905, dedicated to Iris and Rosamund, are grouped in three parts. Headings in the first group speak of things that matter, confession, work, a jilted lover, and a beatific vision, while the second brings mummy wheat, a beech tree, absence, silence, and parting. Only the title pages and contents list are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear.
the-real-mother-goose: Nursery rhymes are gathered under Blanche Fisher Wright's illustrations in an edition dated 1916. A list of rhymes names Little Bo-Peep, Little Boy Blue, Pat-a-Cake, Jack, Solomon Grundy, and many other familiar figures, along with short pieces on rain, clocks, winter, and fingers and toes. Here only the title page and opening of the rhyme list are present, so the rhymes themselves do not appear.
the-secret-rose:
W. B. Yeats dedicated The Secret Rose to A. E. Its contents list the title piece and a dedication poem. Stories follow, including The Crucifixion of the Outcast and The Wisdom of the King. Where There Is Nothing, There Is God is also named. A long tale of Costello the Proud closes the list. Two epigraphs from Villiers de L'Isle Adam and Leonardo da Vinci precede the dedication.

In his letter to A. E., Yeats says the stories share one subject. It is the war of spiritual with natural order, he writes. He wrote them at different times and in different manners, without a definite plan. Irish friends ask when he will write a really national romance, he adds. He answers that poetry comes from looking into the self. That little, infinite, faltering, eternal flame is his source, not famous moments of history.
the-servant-in-the-house: Charles Rann Kennedy's play The Servant in the House is dated 1908 in the front matter shown. Kennedy dedicated it to Walter Hampden. Long quotations from the First Epistle of John follow it. They warn that a man who hates his brother walks in darkness. George Frederick Watts is quoted on the hunger for brotherhood lying beneath modern unrest. The portion shown ends at the heading for the original cast of characters, so no cast or dialogue appears.
the-silent-house: Fergus Hume's The Silent House was published in New York by C. H. Doscher, who held its 1907 copyright. The pages shown give the title matter and contents only. No chapter text follows. The tenant of the silent house opens the list. Shadows on the blind and an unsatisfactory explanation come next. Mrs. Vrain's story and the assurance money follow partway through. Gossip appears at chapter thirteen, where the shown list ends.
the-song-book-of-quong-lee-of-limehouse: Thomas Burke's song book gathers short verses spoken in the voice of Quong Lee of Limehouse, London's old Chinese quarter. Here only the title page and contents have come down. The list runs from Buying and Selling and The Power of Music through pieces on shop windows, lanterns, and tea making. Politicians, gambling, and the Great White War also get their verses, so the poems themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-a-white-rocking-horse: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a white rocking horse, illustrated by Harry L. Smith, is presented here through its title pages and publisher's lists alone. Those lists place the book among the Make Believe stories. The Sawdust Doll, the Lamb on Wheels, and the Bold Tin Soldier stand beside it. Long Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown lists then open. The rocking horse's own adventures do not appear.
the-tale-of-dickie-deer-mouse: Arthur Scott Bailey's animal tale was published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1918, illustrated by Diane Petersen. Only the title pages and a contents list appear in this record. The contents show twelve chapters. A little gentleman hunts a home in them. He meets a startled sleeper and a blackbird's nest. He takes a summer home. He visits the cornfield. He helps Fatty Coon. Dickie Deer Mouse's own adventures do not appear.
the-tale-of-mrs-tittlemouse: Beatrix Potter's Mrs. Tittlemouse was first published by Frederick Warne in 1910, and this record shows a 1985 Penguin impression. The pages present give the title, the publisher's details, and just the first line of the tale, which introduces a wood-mouse named Mrs. Tittlemouse. Her tidy little house, her unwanted visitors, and the spring cleaning that fill the famous story lie beyond what is shown here. Readers get the book's identity and its opening breath, and no more.
the-uninhabited-house:
Charlotte Riddell, an Irish writer of ghost tales, wrote this short tale of a haunted house in 1875. She was the most calm and sure hand at the ghost tale of her age in Britain. Her tale deals with a house no tenant will keep, on a river bank.

A clerk in a law office is paid to lodge in River Hall and break its ill name. By patience and a cool head he works out the fraud and dread that hang on the house. The tale is the quiet peak of the Victorian ghost tale, free of all cheap shock.
the-white-linen-nurse:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott published The White Linen Nurse in 1913, dedicating the little story to Maurice Howe Richardson, who loved romance almost as much as surgery. Chapter one finds the nurse so tired that her noble expression aches. Her head, shoulders, lungs, and ankle-bones ache too, but only the expression feels permanently damaged by three ether-scented years of hospital training.

She studies her bright Nova Scotian reflection in the prim white mirror over her bureau. The face is perfectly good and tidy, she judges, except that it looks disgustingly noble, hygienic, and dollish. Her conscientious sickroom smile hangs like lip-coloured lead from her nose. Abbott opens a romance with its heroine rebelling against her own saintly mask.
the-wise-mamma-goose:
Charlotte B. Herr wrote The Wise Mamma Goose, a children's story published in 1913 with designs by Frances Beem. The book opens with a blank space for a child's name. Mamma Goose has slipped away from a noisy barnyard to think. She hides between tall red hollyhocks in the garden. Thinking, readers learn, has always been hard work for her.

Twelve goslings keep her busy every day. They are soft, round, and fluffy like little yellow balls. Herr compares them proudly with Red Hen's chicks. The goslings find their own breakfasts and love the water. Young readers get a gentle farmyard tale told with warm humor.
the-wooden-horse: Hugh Walpole's The Wooden Horse is shown only through its publication pages in this record. Macmillan first published the novel in April 1909. A new edition followed in 1919, with a portrait of the author. Impressions and a Wayfarers' Library issue came between. No chapter or line of the story itself appears in the pages present here.
theocritus-bion-and-moschus-rendered-int: Andrew Lang rendered the Greek pastoral poets Theocritus, Bion, and Moschus into English prose for Macmillan in 1889. Lang, lately a fellow of Merton College, Oxford, added an introductory essay. The volume is dedicated to Ernest Myers. A contents page lists the essay on Theocritus and his age, then the idyls in order. In this record the listing is where things stop, so Lang's prose versions themselves are not shown.
this-side-of-paradise:
F. Scott Fitzgerald's novel follows Amory Blaine through two books, The Romantic Egotist and The Education of a Personage. Quotations from Rupert Brooke and Oscar Wilde open the volume, which Fitzgerald dedicated to Sigourney Fay. An interlude covers May 1917 to February 1919.

Chapter one presents Amory's parents, Stephen and Beatrice Blaine. Stephen, a Byron-loving man who dozed over encyclopedias, grew rich through two brothers' deaths and met Beatrice at Bar Harbor. Amory inherits his mother's traits and his father's height and wavering. Readers get a debut novel about privilege, romance, and self-invention.
trent-s-last-case: E. C. Bentley dedicates Trent's Last Case, subtitled The Woman in Black, to G. K. Chesterton in a long letter. He owes Chesterton a book in return for The Man Who Was Thursday, he writes. He also unfolded the story's plan to him two years earlier, surrounded by Frenchmen. The contents promise chapters from Bad News and The Inquest to Eruption and Writing a Letter. Only the dedication and contents are present here, so the detective story itself does not appear.
vignettes-in-verse:
Matilda Betham published Vignettes in Verse in 1818. She inscribed the poems to Lady Betham, in respect for her amiable qualities. Her advertisement, dated at Stonkam on May 10 of that year, explains an odd delay. Most of the poems had been printed some two years before. Events seemed set to keep them from ever appearing. Only now has she found the rest of the manuscript.

Reading the whole over, Betham says, struck her with surprise. The verses now look prophetic. She wrote them with a vague, general view. Yet they seem to speak of what has since befallen her: a long seclusion, cut off from the common means of study. That loss gave rise to a pursuit that now fills her life. The first poem plays with journals and wings, each pair of wings a day. Grief and foresight haunt these short pieces from the start.
whitefoot-the-wood-mouse:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote Whitefoot the Wood Mouse, a nature tale for children. Chapter one finds Whitefoot at the end of his happiest winter yet. Whitefoot never lets past troubles spoil the present, Burgess says. He also never borrows worry from the future. That habit keeps him cheerful in a risky life.

Few creatures in the Green Forest face more foes than this small mouse. Buster Bear, Billy Mink, Shadow the Weasel, and Hooty the Owl all hunt him. Foxes and Old Man Coyote watch for him too. He must be ready to run at any moment. Burgess turns wood lore into warm tales of the small and quick.
willie-mouse:
Alta Tabor wrote Willie Mouse, a picture tale for young children from the Saalfield company. Willie Mouse had often heard his mother and father say the moon was made of green cheese. One evening he set out to see if he could find it. The subtitle calls the trip a journey to find the moon.

Willie packs some cheese and a bread crust for the road. He takes his lantern and starts his travels at night. Pictures break up the short lines of text. Tabor gives small readers a gentle quest built on a child's literal belief. A mouse, a lantern, and green cheese carry the tale.
wise-or-otherwise: The pages present here hold title pages and an empty contents heading for Wise or Otherwise, by Lydia Leavitt and Thad. W. H. Leavitt, with no tales shown. The Wells company printed the book in Toronto in 1898. Anna Lake drew the pictures. Lydia Leavitt also wrote Bohemian Society and A Trip Around the World. Her co-author wrote The Witch of Plum Hollow and tales of the gold fields. The book was entered at the Department of Agriculture in 1898, by its copyright line.
words-for-the-wise:
T. S. Arthur published these moral tales in Philadelphia in 1851. His short preface hopes the lessons will warn and guide many readers. The contents promise stories about a poor debtor, a Sunday Christian, and a man who could not get along. Other tales warn against haste to grow rich and against taking things for granted.

The opening story begins with a rich merchant praising one honest man. That man is Moale, a tailor. Each tale turns a small daily failing into a clear lesson. Arthur writes for household readers who want fiction with direct moral use.
zizhi-tongjian-sima-guang-chinese:
Sima Guang, a statesman of the Song court, led a team that spent nineteen years building the Zizhi Tongjian, finished in 1084 CE. Its title means a mirror for aid in ruling. The text here is the complete work, 294 chapters in classical Chinese, from Chinese Wikisource.

Year by year the mirror runs from the Warring States in 403 BCE to the Five Dynasties in 959 CE. Sima Guang chose events for the lessons they taught rulers, and he weighed his sources in open notes. The work is the great year-by-year history of imperial China. Statesmen read it for a thousand years as a handbook of rule.
